meta.blurb: Grace, sixty-three, trips on a kerb. She is not hurt, but she is frightened. Her neighbour Mateo, a physiotherapist, teaches her ten everyday moves, from walking to getting up off the floor, and how to practise each one safely.
meta.bible: Grace: a sixty-three-year-old retired teacher who trips on a kerb and decides to look after her body, the main character. Mateo: her neighbour, a Physiotherapist in his forties, kind, calm and practical; his mother is Rosa, who is seventy-eight and goes to a tai chi class in the park. Dorothy: Grace's friend from number twelve, seventy, funny and a little stubborn. Anna: Grace's grown-up daughter. Leo: Anna's son, Grace's grandson, four years old at the start and five at the end. Dr Okafor: Grace's doctor. Ken: a retired bus driver and joker who joins the Tuesday club; Priya: a neighbour from number five who also joins it; Priya's sister appears at the end. The Tuesday Walkers: the walking club Grace and Dorothy start in spring. Setting: Linden Road, a quiet street of terraced houses, Grace's small garden and kitchen, Millfield Park with a gentle hill and a bench, and the community hall. The charity walk: a five-kilometre community walk in October, in aid of the bandstand. Time: the book runs from one autumn to the next, and the last chapter is one year to the day after the stumble. The ten moves: Walk, Sit to stand, Hinge, Push, Pull, Carry, Climb, Twist, Balance and Floor (down to the floor and back up). Key terms: Kerb, Physiotherapist, Brisk, Posture, Grip, Falls, Tai chi, Flexibility, Stairs, Counter, Hips, Shoulders, Spine, Stretch, Warm-up, Hinge, Repetitions, Intervals, Pedometer, Stamina, Wobble, Rucksack, Treadmill, Hamstrings, Glutes, Quadriceps, Calves, Dietitian, Pharmacist. Facts used: health guidelines suggest about 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days; older adults are also advised to do balance training; about one in three adults over sixty-five falls each year. Voice: warm, simple and encouraging, one idea in each beat, in twenty chapters of ten beats; the ten moves are taught across the middle of the book. The advice is general and hedged: people differ, some conditions need a doctor's advice, and none of it is a diagnosis or a personal plan. This book is general information and is not medical advice.
chapters: What the Body Is Built For
Falls and the Fear of Falling

beats.scene: Grace walks down Linden Road with a shopping list on a grey morning
beats.summary: Grace, a retired teacher of sixty-three, sets out one grey morning to buy bread, her mind on other things.

beats.scene: Grace's foot catches the edge of a kerb and she lurches forward
beats.summary: Her foot catches the edge of a kerb and she pitches forward.

beats.scene: A stranger in a green coat grips Grace's arm beside a lamp post
beats.summary: A passing stranger catches her arm and she grabs a lamp post, and she is not hurt.

beats.scene: Grace walks home slowly with her hand pressed to her chest
beats.summary: She thanks the man, forgets the bread and walks home slowly with her heart pounding.

beats.scene: Grace sits at her kitchen table holding a mug with trembling hands
beats.summary: At home she sits with a cup of tea and remembers how her mother fell years ago.

beats.scene: Grace looks at an empty diary and a sofa dented by long sitting
beats.summary: Grace realises that since she retired she has hardly exercised at all.

beats.scene: Grace stands at the garden fence while Mateo hangs washing on his line
beats.summary: Next morning she meets her neighbour Mateo at the garden fence, and he asks how she is.

beats.scene: Grace talks while Mateo listens, leaning on the fence with his arms folded
beats.summary: Grace tells Mateo about the stumble, and he explains that he is a physiotherapist.

beats.scene: Mateo opens his hands to show how a body can move in many ways
beats.summary: Mateo says that falls are common but not a certain part of ageing, and that the body is built to move.

beats.scene: Grace opens a notebook at the fence while Mateo points to his door
beats.summary: Grace asks him to show her what to do, and he agrees, but first she should talk to her doctor.

beats.scene: Mateo sets two mugs and a notebook on a garden table on Saturday
beats.summary: On Saturday Mateo comes round with a notebook and asks what an ordinary day looks like for Grace.

beats.scene: Grace counts the hours of her day on her fingers at the table
beats.summary: Grace counts up how many hours of her day she spends sitting, and the number surprises her.

beats.scene: A clock beside a chair, with a small figure sitting for hours
beats.summary: Mateo explains that long unbroken sitting is linked with poorer health, and that breaking it up helps.

beats.scene: A heart, a bed and a smiling face drawn on a page
beats.summary: People who are active tend to have healthier hearts and better mood and sleep, though results differ between people.

beats.scene: A weekly calendar with short coloured bars marking walking and strength days
beats.summary: Health guidelines suggest 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strength work on two or more days.

beats.scene: An older couple on a wobbly beam, with a balance symbol above them
beats.summary: For older adults the guidelines add balance training, because balance and strength help prevent falls.

beats.scene: Ten small icons of simple human movements in a ring
beats.summary: Mateo says that almost everything we do in a day is made of about ten basic moves.

beats.scene: Grace writes a list of ten words on a page, her pen moving
beats.summary: He names the ten: walk, sit to stand, hinge, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and getting down to the floor and up again.

beats.scene: Grace sits in a doctor's room while Dr Okafor smiles and nods
beats.summary: Grace sees her doctor, who says she can start and should build up slowly.

beats.scene: Mateo holds up three fingers beside a notebook headed with three rules
beats.summary: Mateo gives her three rules: start small, be regular, and stop if there is sharp pain.

beats.scene: Grace ties her laces at her front door early on a bright Monday
beats.summary: On Monday morning Grace ties her shoes at the door, and Mateo says that walking is the first move.

beats.scene: A person's legs, heart and balance connected by lines as they walk
beats.summary: Walking is the base of all movement: it needs no equipment and uses the legs, the heart and balance.

beats.scene: A pair of firm comfortable shoes on a doormat
beats.summary: Good shoes for walking are comfortable and firm, and they do not need to be expensive.

beats.scene: Grace walks tall with her arms swinging and her eyes on the road
beats.summary: Mateo shows her how to walk well: look ahead, relax the shoulders, swing the arms and let the heel land first.

beats.scene: Two people walking side by side and talking with relaxed faces
beats.summary: A brisk walk is one where you can talk but could not sing, and it counts as moderate activity.

beats.scene: Grace and Mateo walk past a baker's shop and the end of Linden Road
beats.summary: Grace walks ten minutes to the corner and back, and finds it harder than she expected.

beats.scene: Grace pauses to look at the trees and a bird on a garden wall
beats.summary: On the walk Grace notices things she has missed from the car, such as the trees and the baker's window.

beats.scene: Grace writes a number in her notebook with her shoes by the door
beats.summary: Mateo advises that she begin with ten minutes a day and add a little each week.

beats.scene: Grace rubs her tired legs in an armchair after the first week
beats.summary: After the first week her legs are tired, which Mateo says is normal, as long as the feeling is a dull ache and not sharp pain.

beats.scene: Grace sleeps peacefully in bed with sunlight and a notebook beside her
beats.summary: Grace feels a little better in mood, and sleeps better, though Mateo says that people differ.

beats.scene: Grace walks through the gates of Millfield Park with her notebook in her pocket
beats.summary: In the third week she walks for twenty minutes and goes as far as Millfield Park.

beats.scene: Grace and Dorothy walk side by side in coats along a park path
beats.summary: Dorothy, her friend from number twelve, joins her, and they chat easily, which proves the pace is right.

beats.scene: Grace walks fast for a minute and slowly for a minute along a path
beats.summary: Mateo explains intervals: walking fast for a minute and easy for a minute, which can build fitness.

beats.scene: Grace climbs a gentle grassy slope in Millfield Park on a sunny day
beats.summary: Hills count too: a gentle slope makes the legs and heart work a little harder.

beats.scene: Grace walks along a wet street in a bright coat holding an umbrella
beats.summary: On a wet and gloomy day she walks anyway, in a bright coat, and stays careful on slippery ground.

beats.scene: A small counting device clipped to a belt beside a number
beats.summary: Some people count steps; studies suggest benefits grow up to about seven or eight thousand steps a day, but there is no magic number.

beats.scene: A heart with a line showing a steady beat above a walking path
beats.summary: Regular brisk walking is linked with a lower risk of heart disease, though it works best alongside other healthy habits.

beats.scene: Grace sits on a bench in the sun beside green trees
beats.summary: Walking outdoors in daylight and among trees seems to lift people's mood, and Grace feels calmer.

beats.scene: Grace lies on the sofa with her shoes beside the door and a clock
beats.summary: On a lazy morning Grace does not want to go, but Mateo's two-minute rule gets her out of the door.

beats.scene: Grace stands at her gate with a smile and a notebook full of ticks
beats.summary: After a month Grace can walk thirty minutes with a smile, and the first move is done.

beats.scene: Mateo places a plain wooden kitchen chair in the middle of Grace's kitchen
beats.summary: Mateo introduces the second move, sit to stand, using a plain kitchen chair.

beats.scene: A figure rises from a chair, a dotted line showing a squat
beats.summary: Sit to stand is a squat in disguise: we do it from chairs, sofas, cars and toilets all day long.

beats.scene: Grace places her feet under her knees in front of a firm chair
beats.summary: To begin, sit near the front of a firm chair, with feet flat and slightly apart, a little behind the knees.

beats.scene: Grace leans forward with her nose over her toes and stands up
beats.summary: Next lean forward a little, push through your feet, and stand tall.

beats.scene: Grace sits down slowly with her hips back and her hands forward
beats.summary: Sitting back down slowly, with hips back, is as important as standing up.

beats.scene: Grace pushes on the chair arms with both hands to stand up
beats.summary: At first Grace uses her hands to push, and Mateo says that this is fine and that she can do less with practice.

beats.scene: A stopwatch beside a chair on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Mateo describes a common test: how many times you can stand up from a chair in thirty seconds, as a rough guide.

beats.scene: Grace counts aloud while she stands up and sits down again
beats.summary: Grace manages nine stands in thirty seconds, which is a starting point and nothing to worry about.

beats.scene: Grace stands up from her sofa during a television advert
beats.summary: Mateo suggests a habit: stand up slowly from every chair once, or stand during the television adverts.

beats.scene: Dorothy laughs as she stands up from the kitchen chair for the first time
beats.summary: Dorothy hears about it and tries it too, laughing, and finds that she is a little wobbly.

beats.scene: A diagram of big leg and hip muscles glowing in a standing figure
beats.summary: The biggest muscles in the body are in the legs and hips, and they do the work of standing, walking and climbing.

beats.scene: Two sketches of a muscle, one thin and one thick, side by side
beats.summary: Muscle tends to shrink from middle age if it is not used, but it can be built at any age.

beats.scene: Grace lowers herself into a chair very slowly, counting to three
beats.summary: To make sit to stand harder, lower yourself slowly, taking about three seconds to sit down.

beats.scene: Grace stands from a chair holding a bag of rice to her chest
beats.summary: A bag of rice or a full bottle held at the chest adds weight and makes the move harder still.

beats.scene: Grace stands at the kitchen sink with a calendar showing marked days
beats.summary: For strength, two or three days a week is enough, with a rest day in between so the muscles can recover.

beats.scene: A set of small stacked blocks marked with the numbers eight to twelve
beats.summary: A good aim is eight to twelve repetitions, until the muscles feel tired but the movement is still smooth.

beats.scene: Grace rubs her thighs on the stairs the day after exercising
beats.summary: Muscles can be sore a day or two after new exercise, which is normal, but sharp or lasting pain is a warning.

beats.scene: A sturdy bone and a muscle shown pulling together in a leg
beats.summary: Weight-bearing and strength exercise are linked with stronger bones, which matters for avoiding fractures.

beats.scene: A plate of eggs, beans and fish beside a glass of water
beats.summary: Muscles need enough food to repair themselves, including protein; a dietitian can advise on what suits each person.

beats.scene: Grace stands up from the chair quickly while Mateo checks the stopwatch
beats.summary: A month later Grace repeats the test and manages twelve stands, three more than before.

beats.scene: Grace bends over a laundry basket and winces, one hand on her back
beats.summary: Grace picks up a laundry basket with a rounded back and feels a twinge, which leads Mateo to teach the hinge.

beats.scene: A figure bending at the hips like a door on a hinge, back straight
beats.summary: The hinge means bending at the hips, like a door on a hinge, instead of folding the waist.

beats.scene: Grace stands with her hands on her thighs and her hips pushed back
beats.summary: To practise, stand with the feet apart, push the hips back, and slide the hands down the thighs.

beats.scene: Grace holds a broom handle along her spine while bending at the hips
beats.summary: A broom handle along the back helps: it should touch the head, the upper back and the bottom throughout the hinge.

beats.scene: Grace stands up straight with a small smile after a careful hinge
beats.summary: A rounded back is not dangerous in itself, but the hinge is a strong, easy way to lift, and most people can learn it.

beats.scene: Grace reaches for a low kitchen shelf with a tidy hinge
beats.summary: Grace practises by reaching a low shelf in the kitchen, and soon the hinge feels natural.

beats.scene: Grace lifts a bag of compost close to her body in a garden
beats.summary: To lift, keep the load close to the body, breathe steadily, and stand up using the legs and hips.

beats.scene: Grace kneels beside her flower bed and bends carefully to weed
beats.summary: In the garden the hinge helps with weeding, planting and moving pots, and kneeling or sitting on a stool is fine too.

beats.scene: Mateo and Grace sit talking about back pain in the sunny living room
beats.summary: Back pain is very common and most episodes improve; staying gently active usually helps, but severe or unusual symptoms need a doctor.

beats.scene: Grace lifts a full basket from the floor and smiles at Mateo
beats.summary: A week later Grace lifts the laundry basket with a smooth hinge and no twinge at all.

beats.scene: Grace pushes a stiff front door with her shoulder in the cold
beats.summary: Grace's front door sticks in the damp weather, and Mateo says that pushing is the fourth move.

beats.scene: Figures pushing a door, a trolley and a lawn mower
beats.summary: Pushing is part of daily life: doors, trolleys, lawnmowers, prams and getting up from the floor.

beats.scene: Grace stands an arm's length from a wall with her hands flat on it
beats.summary: The gentlest push-up is against a wall: stand an arm's length away, hands flat at shoulder height.

beats.scene: Grace bends her elbows and brings her chest close to the wall
beats.summary: Bend the elbows to bring the chest towards the wall, then push back to the start, breathing out as you push.

beats.scene: Grace does a press-up with her hands on a kitchen worktop
beats.summary: To make the push-up harder, use a worktop or a low table, and later the floor, going on when you are ready.

beats.scene: A body diagram with chest, shoulders and arms glowing as she pushes
beats.summary: The push works the chest, the shoulders and the back of the arms, and also the stomach muscles that hold the body straight.

beats.scene: Grace lifts a tin of beans onto a high kitchen shelf with straight arms
beats.summary: Pushing a light weight overhead, like putting tins on a high shelf, trains the shoulders, but should be done carefully.

beats.scene: Grace pushes a full supermarket trolley across a car park
beats.summary: Daily pushes count as training too: a loaded trolley, a lawnmower or a heavy door all use the same muscles.

beats.scene: Grace stops with a hand on her shoulder as Mateo nods in concern
beats.summary: If a shoulder pinches or hurts sharply when pushing, stop and ask a professional rather than pushing through it.

beats.scene: Grace writes numbers in her notebook next to her kitchen counter
beats.summary: Grace counts her wall push-ups in her notebook and reaches fifteen, with her grandson Leo pushing the wall too.

beats.scene: Grace pulls a heavy glass shop door open with both hands in the rain
beats.summary: On a rainy day Grace struggles with a heavy shop door, and Mateo says that pulling is the fifth move.

beats.scene: Figures pulling a door, a rope and a bag towards their bodies
beats.summary: Pulling includes opening doors, drawing a bag towards you, hauling a rope and starting a lawnmower.

beats.scene: A woman at a desk hunched forward and then sitting upright
beats.summary: Many of us spend hours with rounded shoulders; a stronger upper back helps posture, though no posture is perfect.

beats.scene: Grace pulls a rubber band toward her chest with her elbows back
beats.summary: A resistance band tied to a door handle makes a simple row: pull the elbows back and squeeze the shoulder blades.

beats.scene: Grace leans on a chair and pulls a bag up towards her ribs
beats.summary: A one-arm row with a bag of shopping, with the free hand on a chair, trains the back without special equipment.

beats.scene: Grace hangs washing on a line, pulling a sheet taut
beats.summary: Everyday pulls count as practice: hanging washing, pulling weeds, opening a stiff drawer or a car boot.

beats.scene: Two arrows, one pushing and one pulling, balanced on a seesaw
beats.summary: As a rule of thumb, balance each push with a pull, so the shoulders are trained evenly.

beats.scene: Dorothy stands with her shoulders back, holding a rubber band
beats.summary: Dorothy, who has round shoulders, tries the band too and finds it surprisingly hard.

beats.scene: Grace stands taller in her hallway mirror with her shoulders open
beats.summary: After some weeks Grace notices that she stands a little taller, though Mateo says that many things contribute.

beats.scene: Mateo and Grace smile at a garden table with a cake and a band
beats.summary: Mateo says that she has now met five of the ten moves, and they celebrate with tea and cake.

beats.scene: Grace walks uphill with two heavy bags and her shoulders pulled down
beats.summary: Grace struggles home with heavy shopping, and Mateo introduces the sixth move, the carry.

beats.scene: Figures carrying a suitcase, a child and a pile of washing
beats.summary: Carrying means lifting something and walking with it: shopping, suitcases, laundry and grandchildren.

beats.scene: Grace walks with a filled watering can in each hand, standing tall
beats.summary: The simplest way to train is to carry a weight in each hand, standing tall, taking short steady steps.

beats.scene: A hand squeezes a ball next to a drawing of a strong handshake
beats.summary: Grip strength is linked in studies with general health, though that does not mean that grip alone causes it.

beats.scene: A kitchen scale with a bag and a bottle, and a notebook with numbers
beats.summary: Begin with a light load and a short distance, such as two full water bottles to the gate, and add a little at a time.

beats.scene: Grace carries one heavy bag in her right hand, leaning slightly to the left
beats.summary: Carrying a load in one hand makes the trunk work to stay upright; switch hands often.

beats.scene: Grace lowers herself with a hinge to hug her grandson Leo
beats.summary: Leo asks to be picked up, and Grace lifts him with a good hinge, keeping him close.

beats.scene: Grace packs two small shopping bags instead of one big bag
beats.summary: Packing the shopping into two smaller bags that weigh about the same makes carrying easier and safer.

beats.scene: Grace wears a rucksack with both straps on, standing tall
beats.summary: A rucksack worn on both shoulders keeps the load close to the back and spreads the weight evenly.

beats.scene: Grace and Mateo and Dorothy drink tea in the garden beside two watering cans
beats.summary: At the half-way point, Grace carries two filled watering cans the length of the garden and reaches six of the ten moves.

beats.scene: Grace stands at the bottom of her staircase and looks up
beats.summary: Grace pauses at the foot of her own staircase, and Mateo introduces the seventh move, climbing.

beats.scene: Figures climbing stairs, a hillside path and a kerb
beats.summary: Climbing covers stairs, steps, slopes and kerbs, and it makes the legs, heart and lungs work hard.

beats.scene: Grace holds a stair rail with a good light above the steps
beats.summary: Before practising, make the stairs safe: good light, a firm handrail, nothing on the steps and shoes or socks with grip.

beats.scene: Grace steps up onto the bottom stair and down again with a smile
beats.summary: Practise with step-ups: step onto the bottom stair, stand tall, and step down, then repeat leading with the other foot.

beats.scene: A heart and lungs glowing beside a short flight of stairs
beats.summary: Studies suggest that short bursts of stair climbing during the day can improve fitness, so a few flights count.

beats.scene: Grace goes carefully down the stairs holding the rail with one hand
beats.summary: Going down needs control: slow steps, the whole foot on each stair, and the eyes on the stairs.

beats.scene: Grace rubs her knee gently on a stair while Mateo kneels beside her
beats.summary: If knees ache on stairs, strengthening the legs often helps, but lasting pain should be checked by a professional.

beats.scene: Grace walks up the gentle hill in Millfield Park with short steps
beats.summary: On a hill, take short steps, lean slightly forward from the ankles and let the arms swing to keep the rhythm.

beats.scene: Grace counts her breaths on the stairs with a notebook on the rail
beats.summary: Use the talk test on stairs and hills: breathing hard is normal, but being unable to speak or feeling dizzy means stop.

beats.scene: Grace stands at the top of the hill looking at the town and smiling
beats.summary: At the top of the hill Grace looks at the town and counts seven moves done, with the three hardest to come.

beats.scene: Grace twists in the driver's seat of a parked car, wincing at her neck
beats.summary: Reversing her car, Grace finds that she cannot turn her body far enough, and Mateo introduces the eighth move, the twist.

beats.scene: Figures turning to look behind, reaching for a seat belt and sweeping
beats.summary: A twist is turning the upper body: looking behind you, reaching for a seat belt, sweeping or swinging a golf club.

beats.scene: Grace sits tall on a chair with her arms crossed over her chest
beats.summary: The seated twist: sit tall, cross the arms over the chest, and slowly turn the upper body from side to side.

beats.scene: A spine drawn in the middle with arrows showing a smooth turn
beats.summary: The turn should come from the chest and ribs, not the lower back or the knees, and it should never be forced.

beats.scene: Grace turns with a light bag of rice held out in front of her
beats.summary: A standing twist with a light weight, such as a bag of rice held at chest height, adds a little strength.

beats.scene: A ring of muscles around a waist, glowing while a figure carries a bag
beats.summary: The core muscles around the middle also resist twisting, which is why carrying a bag on one side trains them.

beats.scene: Grace stretches her arms gently after a walk in the park
beats.summary: A few gentle stretches after exercise, when the muscles are warm, can help a person feel looser, and each should be held for about thirty seconds.

beats.scene: A question mark above a stretching figure, with a doctor and a coach nodding
beats.summary: Research on whether stretching prevents injury is mixed, but it can help people feel looser, so it is a matter of choice.

beats.scene: Grace and Dorothy dance a slow waltz in the community hall
beats.summary: Dorothy takes Grace to a tea dance, where the turns and steps are good for twisting, balance and spirits.

beats.scene: Grace reverses her car smoothly out of the drive with a clear view
beats.summary: A month later Grace reverses out of the drive easily, turning her head and shoulders to see behind.

beats.scene: Grace stands on one leg while brushing her teeth in the bathroom
beats.summary: Mateo introduces the ninth move, balance, with a trick: stand on one leg while brushing your teeth.

beats.scene: A head with eyes, an ear and feet, joined by lines to the brain
beats.summary: Balance depends on the eyes, the inner ear, and the feelings from the feet and joints, all combined by the brain.

beats.scene: A line on a graph sloping downward beside a rising one for practice
beats.summary: Balance tends to decline with age if it is not practised, but it can be trained at any age.

beats.scene: Grace stands on one foot beside a kitchen counter, hand lightly touching it
beats.summary: Start near a counter: lift one foot a little, hold for ten seconds, and keep a hand close in case you wobble.

beats.scene: Grace stands on one foot with just one finger resting on the counter
beats.summary: As it gets easier, use fewer fingers, then no hands, and later try a softer surface or a longer hold.

beats.scene: Grace walks a straight line heel to toe along a hallway floor
beats.summary: Walking heel to toe in a straight line, as if on a tightrope, is another good balance exercise, with a wall for safety.

beats.scene: Grace walks on grass and turns her head slowly to look around
beats.summary: Walking on grass, turning the head, and stepping over small objects all challenge balance in useful ways.

beats.scene: Mateo's mother Rosa does slow tai chi movements in the park in the morning
beats.summary: Mateo's mother Rosa, aged seventy-eight, practises tai chi, which has good evidence for reducing falls.

beats.scene: Grace stands in a circle of older people in the park, arms raised
beats.summary: At her first tai chi class Grace moves slowly, holds a pose, wobbles and laughs, and feels calmer afterwards.

beats.scene: Grace stands steadily on one leg in the garden, holding her arms out
beats.summary: After a month of practice Grace can stand on one leg for twenty seconds, and that is nine moves met, with only one left.

beats.scene: A street with older people walking carefully and a sign about falls
beats.summary: About one in three adults over sixty-five falls each year; most falls do not cause serious injury, but some do.

beats.scene: Mateo draws a list of changeable causes beside a thoughtful Grace
beats.summary: Falls are not just a normal part of ageing: strength, balance, eyesight, medicines and the home can all be improved.

beats.scene: Mateo and Grace walk through the rooms of her house looking at the floors
beats.summary: Mateo and Grace do a home safety walk, looking for loose rugs, cables, dim lights and slippery floors.

beats.scene: Grace tapes down a rug beside a bright night light in the hall
beats.summary: Grace removes the loose rug, tidies the cable, adds a night light and puts a non-slip mat in the bathroom.

beats.scene: A pair of firm slippers beside loose old slippers on a floor mat
beats.summary: Footwear matters: loose slippers and socks on slippery floors can cause trips, and shoes with grip are safer.

beats.scene: Grace reads a letter chart at an optician's with a friendly assistant
beats.summary: Eyesight changes can raise the risk of falling, so regular eye tests are worth having, and bifocals need care on stairs.

beats.scene: A pharmacist's counter with a person asking questions and a neat pile of boxes
beats.summary: Some medicines can cause dizziness, so a person should ask a pharmacist or doctor and never stop a medicine alone.

beats.scene: Grace stands slowly from a chair and pauses, a hand on the table
beats.summary: Standing up slowly helps with dizziness on rising; frequent or severe dizziness should be seen by a doctor.

beats.scene: Mateo and Grace read a leaflet showing exercises for strength and balance
beats.summary: Programmes that combine strength and balance training have the best evidence for lowering the risk of falls, three days a week is a common aim.

beats.scene: Grace sits with Mateo, a mug, and a drawing of a circle of arrows
beats.summary: Fear of falling can make people move less, which makes them weaker and more likely to fall, and Mateo helps Grace to break this circle.

beats.scene: Mateo asks a laughing Grace when she last sat on the living-room floor
beats.summary: Mateo asks Grace when she last sat on the floor, and she cannot remember.

beats.scene: A figure sitting on a floor looking up at an empty chair
beats.summary: Getting down and up is a real skill; a person who cannot get up after a fall is in a worse position, and floor play and gardening need it too.

beats.scene: A soft mat, a sturdy sofa and a clear space in a living room
beats.summary: Prepare a safe space: a soft mat, a sturdy sofa or chair, a clear floor, and someone nearby for the first attempts.

beats.scene: Grace kneels on one knee with a hand on the sofa seat
beats.summary: The first step is a half-kneel: put a hand on the sofa, step one foot back, and lower that knee gently to the floor.

beats.scene: Grace lowers both knees onto the mat and sits to one side
beats.summary: Next bring the other knee down, put both hands on the floor, and sit gently to one side, taking your time.

beats.scene: Grace sits happily on the mat with her legs stretched out in front
beats.summary: Once down, Grace sits in a comfortable position, such as legs stretched out or crossed, and enjoys a different view of the room.

beats.scene: Grace puts a cushion under her knee and a hand on the sofa
beats.summary: A cushion under the knees, forearms on a chair, or a lower sofa can make getting down easier, and there is no shame in using them.

beats.scene: Grace sits on the mat looking proud with Mateo giving a thumbs up
beats.summary: Grace goes down and sits on the floor on her own, and Mateo cheers.

beats.scene: Leo runs into the living room with a box of wooden blocks
beats.summary: Leo arrives with a box of blocks, and Grace realises that she wants to play with him on the floor.

beats.scene: Grace and Leo build a tall tower of blocks on the floor

B1B2: Grace is sixty-three and a retired teacher, and she lives on a quiet street of terraced houses. One grey morning she sets out for the baker's, her mind full of lists and small worries.
Her toe catches the edge of the kerb and the pavement rushes up to meet her. For a moment she cannot even put out her hands.
A man in a green coat catches her arm just in time, and she grabs a lamp post with her other hand. She stands there, breathing hard, with nothing hurt but her pride.
She thanks the man, forgets all about the bread and walks slowly home. Her heart is still pounding, and her legs feel strangely weak.
At home she makes a cup of tea, but her hands shake as she lifts it. She remembers her mother, who fell in her eighties and never walked well again.
Grace thinks back over her week and realises how little she has moved since she retired. She walks to the car, sits in the car and sits again at home.
The next morning Grace is in the garden when her neighbour Mateo waves from the other side of the fence. He is hanging out his washing, and he asks cheerfully how she is.
Grace tells him about the kerb and the lamp post and the frightening feeling in her stomach. Mateo listens carefully, and then he says that he is a physiotherapist.
Mateo says that stumbles are common but that falls are not simply a fact of getting older. The human body, he tells her, is built to move, and it stays good at moving if we keep using it.
Grace asks if he could show her what to do, and Mateo happily agrees. He asks for one thing first, which is that she talks to her doctor about her plans.
On Saturday morning Mateo arrives with a notebook and two mugs of coffee. He asks Grace to describe an ordinary day, from the moment she wakes up.
Grace counts on her fingers as she talks: breakfast, the radio, the car, the television. By the end she has found that she sits for nearly ten hours a day.
Mateo explains that large studies link long hours of sitting with poorer health. They cannot prove that sitting is the only cause, but it helps to stand up and walk around often.
Regular activity is linked with a healthier heart, stronger muscles and bones, and often with better sleep and mood. These effects vary between people, but on average they are real and they add up.

Health guidelines for adults suggest about 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity each week. They also advise muscle-strengthening exercise on two or more days, and some movement is always better than none.
For older adults the guidelines add something extra, which is balance practice. Balance and strength together are the best defence against falls, and both can be trained at any age.
Mateo says that nearly everything we do in a day is made of about ten basic movements. If we keep those ten in good shape, ordinary life stays easy.

He lists them slowly while she writes: walk, sit to stand, hinge, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and floor. Some of the words are strange to her, but he promises that each one will make sense.
On Monday Grace visits Dr Okafor and explains her plan. The doctor checks her blood pressure, asks a few questions, and says that she can start, as long as she builds up slowly.
Mateo gives her three simple rules for the weeks ahead. Start small, be regular rather than heroic, and stop at once if something hurts sharply.
On Monday morning Grace ties her shoes at the front door, and Mateo joins her on the path. The first move, he says, is the oldest and simplest of all, and it is walking.
Walking costs nothing and needs no equipment, yet it works the legs, the heart and the sense of balance. For most people it is the best place to begin.
Mateo checks her shoes and decides that they are fine. He says that walking shoes should be comfortable, with a firm sole and enough room for the toes, and that they need not be expensive.
Mateo shows her how to walk with better posture. She should look ahead rather than down, keep her shoulders loose and her arms swinging, and let each heel land first.
How fast should she walk, Grace asks him as they set off. Mateo explains the talk test: at a brisk pace you can speak in sentences, but you could not sing a song.
Grace and Mateo walk to the corner of Linden Road and back, which takes about ten minutes. She is a little out of breath, and she is surprised that something so ordinary feels so hard.
On foot she sees things that she has never noticed from the car. The cherry tree is already turning yellow, and the baker's window smells wonderful.
Mateo advises her to begin with ten minutes a day, and to add a few minutes each week. Slow and steady, he says, is how bodies learn.
By the end of the first week she has walked on six days, and her legs feel tired. Mateo says that a dull tiredness is normal, but a sharp pain is not.
After two weeks Grace feels more cheerful, and she is sleeping better at night. Mateo says that many people notice this, although not everyone does.
By the third week Grace is walking for twenty minutes, and her route has grown. She now goes all the way to the gates of Millfield Park.
Her friend Dorothy from number twelve spots her in the park and decides to join her. They chat the whole way round, which, as Grace tells her, shows that the pace is exactly right.
Mateo shows her a clever trick for longer walks called intervals. She walks fast for one minute and then slowly for one minute, and she repeats this several times to build up her fitness.
Millfield Park has a gentle hill, and Grace decides to walk up it on her way home. Slopes make the heart and legs work harder, so even a small one counts.
On a rainy day Grace wears a bright coat and walks anyway. She keeps to the pavement, steps carefully on wet leaves, and is glad that she went.
Mateo says that some people enjoy counting their steps with a small device. Studies suggest that benefits grow up to roughly seven or eight thousand steps a day, but there is no magic number.
Regular brisk walking is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Mateo adds that it works best alongside other healthy habits, and that nobody can promise a result for one person.
Grace has started to look forward to the park. Time outdoors in daylight, among trees, seems to lift many people's mood, and she feels calmer than she has in a long time.
One grey morning Grace does not feel like walking at all. Mateo has a trick for such days: put on your shoes and walk for just two minutes, and then decide.
After a month Grace can walk for thirty minutes without stopping, and her notebook is full of ticks. Mateo says that the first move is now in good shape and that it is time for the second.
Mateo puts a plain wooden chair in the middle of Grace's kitchen floor. The second move, he says, is one that she has done thousands of times without thinking: sit to stand.
Sit to stand is really a squat in disguise. We do it from chairs, sofas, car seats and toilets all day, and the ability to do it keeps people independent.
Mateo shows her carefully how to set up the chair. She sits near the front of a firm chair, with her feet flat on the floor, about hip-width apart and just behind her knees.
Then she leans forward from the hips until her nose is over her toes. Pushing down through her feet, she rises until she stands tall.
Sitting down slowly is just as important as standing up. She pushes her hips back, bends her knees, and lowers herself slowly instead of dropping into the seat.
At first Grace pushes on her knees to get up, and she feels a little ashamed. Mateo tells her that there is nothing wrong with that, and that she can use her hands less as she gets stronger.
Mateo describes a common test of leg strength that therapists use. He times thirty seconds while Grace stands up as often as she can, and he says that the number is only a rough guide.
Mateo starts the clock and Grace counts aloud as she stands up and sits down. She manages nine stands in thirty seconds, and he writes it in the notebook as her starting point.
Mateo suggests a little habit that costs nothing at all. Whenever she gets up from a chair she can do it slowly and well, and she can practise during the television adverts.
Dorothy comes round for tea and wants to try the exercise too. She laughs as her legs shake a little, and then she asks for a go at the thirty-second test.
The biggest muscles in the body are in the thighs and buttocks. They do most of the work when we stand, walk and climb, so it pays to keep them strong.
Muscle tends to shrink slowly from middle age if we do not use it. The good news is that it can be built up again at any age, even in a person's eighties and nineties.
To make the move harder, Grace lowers herself slowly, counting to three on the way down. Her thighs begin to burn, and she smiles because it means that the muscles are working.
Another way to make it harder is to hold something heavy. Grace holds a bag of rice against her chest as she stands, and she feels the difference at once.
Strength work is not meant for every single day. Two or three days a week is enough, with a rest day in between so that the muscles can recover and grow stronger.
A good aim is eight to twelve repetitions in a row, which is called a set. By the end the muscles should feel tired, but the movement should still be smooth and safe.
The next day Grace's legs are sore, and she walks down the stairs rather stiffly. Mateo says that this soreness is normal after new exercise, but that sharp or lasting pain is a different matter.
Exercise helps the bones as well as the muscles. Activities that load the body, such as walking and strength work, are linked with stronger bones and so with fewer broken bones in later life.
Muscles need good food to repair themselves, and that includes enough protein. Mateo adds that people's needs differ, and that a dietitian can give advice that suits a particular person.
A month later Mateo times her again, with the stopwatch in his hand. This time Grace manages twelve stands in thirty seconds, three more than before, and she never uses her hands.
Grace bends over to pick up a heavy laundry basket and feels a twinge in her back. Mateo, who is watching from the fence, says that it is time to learn the third move.
The hinge means bending forward at the hips, like a door swinging on its hinge. The big muscles of the buttocks and thighs do the work instead of the small muscles of the back.
To practise, Grace stands with her feet hip-width apart and her hands on her thighs. She pushes her hips back as if closing a car door with her bottom, and her knees bend a little.
Mateo gives her a broom handle to hold along her back, touching her head, her upper back and her tailbone. If all three stay in contact as she hinges, her spine is staying long and steady.
A rounded back is not automatically dangerous, Mateo says, and the spine is tougher than we think. The hinge is simply a strong and efficient way to bend, and most people can learn it quickly.
Grace practises the hinge by reaching for a pan on a low shelf. After a few tries the movement begins to feel natural, and her back no longer protests.

When lifting a heavy bag, Mateo says, hold it close to the body, because a load far from the body is much harder to control. She should breathe steadily and stand up by pushing through her legs and hips.
In the garden the hinge helps with weeding, planting and moving pots. When it is too tiring, Grace can kneel on a mat or sit on a low stool instead, and there is no shame in that.
Back pain is very common, and most episodes improve within weeks. Staying gently active usually helps, but severe pain, numbness or weakness in a leg should be checked by a doctor.
A week later Grace lifts the very same laundry basket from the floor. This time she hinges at the hips, keeps the basket close, and feels no twinge at all.
Grace's front door sticks in the damp weather, and she has to shove it with her shoulder. Mateo tells her that pushing is the fourth of the ten moves.
We push all day long without ever thinking about it. Doors, trolleys, lawnmowers, prams and wheelchairs all ask the muscles of the chest, shoulders and arms to press forward.
The gentlest kind of push-up is done standing against a wall. Grace stands about an arm's length away, puts her hands flat on the wall at shoulder height, and keeps her feet on the floor.
Grace bends her elbows and lowers her chest towards the wall, then pushes herself back to the start. Mateo reminds her to breathe out as she pushes and to keep her body in a straight line.
To make the push-up harder, Grace can move her hands to a kitchen counter or a low table. The lower the surface, the more of her body weight she has to push.
A push works the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms. It also asks the stomach muscles to keep the body in a straight line, so it trains much more than the arms.
Pushing a light weight overhead, like putting tins on a high shelf, also trains the shoulders. Mateo says to go slowly, keep the ribs down, and avoid arching the back.
Daily pushes count as training too, Mateo reminds her. When Grace pushes a full trolley or a mower across the grass, she is using the muscles from her wall press-ups.
If a shoulder pinches or hurts sharply during a push, Grace should stop and ask a professional. Pushing through real pain, Mateo says, is never a good idea.
Grace writes her wall push-ups in her notebook, and by the end of the week she reaches fifteen. Her four-year-old grandson Leo visits and decides to push the wall too.
On a rainy day Grace has to pull hard on a heavy shop door with both hands. Mateo, who is with her, says that she has just shown him the fifth move, which is the pull.
Pulling includes opening doors, drawing a bag towards you, hauling on a rope and starting a lawnmower. It uses the muscles of the back and the front of the arms.
Many of us spend hours at a desk or a screen with our shoulders rounded. A strong upper back can help us sit and stand more comfortably, although no single posture is perfect.
A long rubber band tied around a door handle makes a simple row. Grace holds the ends, pulls her elbows back and gently squeezes her shoulder blades together.
Another version of the pull needs only a bag of shopping. With one hand on a chair for support, Grace pulls the bag up towards her ribs, lowers it slowly and then changes sides.
Everyday pulls count as useful practice too, as Grace soon finds. Hanging out washing, pulling up weeds, opening a stiff drawer and lifting a bag from a car boot all use the same muscles.
As a rule of thumb, Mateo says, she should balance every pushing exercise with a pulling one. In that way the muscles around the shoulders are trained evenly.
Dorothy, who has rather round shoulders from years of sewing, wants to try the band as well. She finds it much harder than she expected, and Grace has to hold back a grin.
After some weeks of rowing, Grace notices that she stands a little taller. Mateo says that many things contribute to posture, but she is delighted all the same.
Five of the ten moves are done, and Mateo says that this calls for a celebration. They sit in the garden with tea and a slice of lemon cake.
On the way home from the market Grace is carrying two heavy bags, and her arms are aching. Mateo meets her at the gate and says that she is doing the sixth move, which is the carry.
To carry means to lift something and walk with it. Shopping, suitcases, baskets of washing and grandchildren are all part of life, and they all ask a lot of the body.
The simplest way to train is to carry a weight in each hand. Grace fills two watering cans, stands tall with her shoulders down, and walks across the garden in short, steady steps.
Studies link a strong grip with better health in later life. That does not prove that grip itself causes good health, but it shows how a strong hand reflects a strong body.
Mateo says to begin with a light load and a short distance, such as two full water bottles carried to the gate. She can add a little more weight or distance each week.
Carrying a bag in one hand is harder in a different way, because the trunk has to work to stay upright. Mateo tells her to switch hands often and to keep her shoulders level.
Her grandson Leo comes to visit and holds up his arms to be lifted. Grace hinges at the hips, keeps him close to her chest, and stands up using her legs.
Grace learns to pack her shopping into two smaller bags of about the same weight. They are easier to carry than one big bag, and her body stays balanced.
Mateo also recommends a good rucksack for longer trips to the shops. Worn on both shoulders, it keeps the load close to the back and spreads the weight evenly.
At the end of the chapter Grace carries two filled watering cans to the end of the garden and back without stopping. Six of the ten moves are now part of her life, and Dorothy cheers.
Grace stops at the bottom of her own staircase and looks up at it. Mateo, who has come in for tea, says that the seventh move is climbing.
Climbing covers stairs, steps, slopes and even the humble kerb. It asks the legs, the heart and the lungs to work harder than walking on flat ground does.
First, Mateo checks that her stairs are safe to use. There must be a good light, a firm handrail, nothing left on the steps and sensible footwear instead of loose slippers.
A good way to practise on stairs is the step-up. Grace places one whole foot on the bottom stair, stands up tall on it, and then steps carefully back down, holding the rail.
Some studies suggest that short bursts of stair climbing, spread across the day, can improve fitness. Even a few flights count, which is encouraging for someone with a staircase at home.
Going down the stairs is harder than going up, because the legs must control the body's weight. Grace goes one step at a time, with a hand on the rail and her eyes on her feet.
Grace's knees feel a little stiff after the stairs. Mateo says that stronger legs often help the knees, but that lasting or sharp pain should be looked at by a professional.
On the hill in Millfield Park, Mateo shows her how to take short steps and lean a little forward from the ankles. Letting her arms swing helps her to keep a steady rhythm.
The talk test works on stairs and hills too. It is normal to breathe hard, but if Grace cannot speak at all, or feels dizzy, she must stop and rest.
At the top of the hill Grace turns and looks down at the whole town. Seven of the ten moves are now hers, and she feels as if she has climbed a great deal more than a hill.
While reversing the car Grace finds it hard to look over her shoulder, and she has to stop. Mateo says that this is the eighth move, which is the twist.
A twist is a turn of the upper body, and we use it more than we realise. We twist to look behind us, to fasten a seat belt, to sweep a floor or to hit a golf ball.
The seated twist is a gentle place to start. Grace sits tall, folds her arms across her chest, and slowly turns to look over one shoulder and then the other.
The turn should come mostly from the chest and upper back, not from the lower back or the knees. It should never be forced, and a gentle stretch is always enough.
A standing twist adds a little more strength to the move. Grace holds a light bag of rice at chest height and turns slowly from side to side with her hips still.
The muscles around the middle, often called the core, also work to stop the body from twisting. That is why carrying a bag on one side is such good training for them.
After a walk, when her muscles are warm, Grace learns a few gentle stretches. Mateo says to hold each one for about thirty seconds, until she feels a mild pull but no pain.
Does stretching really prevent injury, Dorothy asks, and must she do it every day? The evidence is mixed, Mateo admits, but it can help people feel looser, so it is a matter of personal choice.
Dorothy takes Grace to a tea dance at the community hall. The slow turns and the steps are good for twisting, for balance and for the spirits, and they laugh all afternoon.
A month later Grace backs her car out of the drive without any trouble. She turns her head and shoulders far enough to see behind her, and she feels much safer.
Mateo introduces the ninth move, which is balance, with a very simple trick. Grace should stand on one leg for a minute while she brushes her teeth, holding the sink if she needs to.
Balance depends on three things working together: the eyes, the inner ear and the feelings from our feet and joints. The brain combines all of them every second, without our noticing.
Balance tends to decline with age if it is not practised. The good news, Mateo says, is that it can be trained at any age, and that improvement often comes within a few weeks.
Mateo shows her how to start, near a kitchen counter. She lifts one foot a few centimetres, holds the counter lightly, and counts to ten before changing legs.
As the exercise gets easier, Grace uses fewer fingers on the counter, and later no hands at all. Mateo says to keep the counter close, and to make it harder only a little at a time.
Walking heel to toe is another good balance exercise. Grace walks along a hallway, putting the heel of one foot against the toes of the other, as though she were crossing a tightrope.
Everyday walking can challenge your balance too, as Mateo explains. Walking on grass, turning the head to look around, and stepping over small objects all make the body work a little harder.
Mateo's mother Rosa is seventy-eight, and she practises tai chi in the park every Wednesday. Mateo explains that this slow and gentle exercise has good evidence for reducing falls in older people.
At her first tai chi class Grace moves slowly with a dozen other people. She wobbles, laughs, and feels calmer by the end of the hour than she has for weeks.
After a month of practice Grace can stand on one leg for twenty seconds without holding anything. Nine of the ten moves have now been met, and only one is left.
About one in three adults over sixty-five falls at least once a year. Most falls do not cause serious injury, Mateo says, but some do, and that is why prevention matters.
Falls are not simply a normal part of getting older. Strength, balance, eyesight, medicines and the state of the home are all things that can be improved.
Mateo and Grace walk through her house looking for hazards. They find loose rugs, a trailing cable on the landing, a dim bulb in the hall and a slippery mat in the bathroom.
Grace removes the loose rug, tidies the cable, fits a brighter bulb and puts a night light on the landing. In the bathroom she adds a non-slip mat and a grab rail.
Footwear matters a great deal too, Mateo tells her firmly. Loose slippers, or socks on a smooth floor, can cause a slip, whereas shoes that fit well and grip the floor are much safer.
Eyesight changes can raise the risk of a fall. Grace books an eye test, and the optician reminds her that glasses with two strengths need extra care on stairs.
Some medicines can make people feel dizzy or sleepy. Mateo says that anyone who worries should ask a pharmacist or a doctor, and should never stop a medicine without advice.
Some people feel light-headed when they stand up quickly. Mateo advises Grace to rise slowly and to pause for a moment, and to see her doctor if the dizziness is frequent.
Mateo says that programmes combining strength and balance training have the best evidence for lowering the risk of a fall. Aiming for about three days a week is common advice.
Mateo explains a circle that many people fall into. Fear of falling makes them move less, so they grow weaker and fall more easily, but Grace has already broken out of the circle.
Mateo asks Grace a simple question: when did she last sit on the floor? She laughs, and then she realises that she cannot remember at all.
Getting down to the floor and up again is a real skill. People who can do it are less afraid of falling, and they can play with children, garden and pick up what they drop.
First they prepare a safe space for the practice. They lay a soft mat beside a sturdy sofa, clear the floor, and agree that Mateo will stay close for the first attempts.
The first step on the way down is to half-kneel. Grace puts a hand on the sofa, steps one foot back and lowers that knee gently onto the mat.
Next Grace brings her other knee down and puts both hands on the mat. She then lowers her hip and sits to one side, taking as much time as she needs.
Once she is down, Grace tries a few comfortable positions, with her legs stretched out or crossed. The room looks quite different from down here, and she laughs at the dust under the sofa.
If her knees feel sore, Grace can put a cushion under them, or she can lean on a chair with her forearms. There is no shame in using any help that makes the move safer.
The following week Grace goes down to the floor by herself, slowly and carefully. When she is sitting on the mat, Mateo gives a cheer that makes the neighbours jump.
Leo arrives with his mother Anna, carrying a big box of wooden blocks. When he tips them onto the carpet, Grace realises that she wants to play on the floor with him.
Grace and Leo build a very tall tower of blocks together, and they laugh when it falls down. Anna watches from the sofa, and she is surprised to see her mother so easily down on the floor.
Grace is sitting on the carpet with Leo, and it is time to get up again. Mateo, who is standing by the sofa, says that she can do it in five calm steps.
The first step is to roll onto one side and then onto the hands and knees. Grace pauses there for a moment to check that she feels well and that nothing hurts.
Next, Grace crawls to the sturdy sofa and places both hands flat on the seat. The sofa is heavy and solid, and it will not slide away from her.
Then she brings her stronger leg forward and puts the foot flat on the floor, with her knee bent. She is in the half-kneeling position again, and her hands are still on the seat.
Next she pushes down through her hands and her front foot and rises slowly. When she is standing, she turns around and sits down on the sofa with a long breath.
Getting up from the floor is tiring at first, and Grace sits on the sofa to breathe for a while. Mateo says that speed does not matter, and that only safety and control are important.
Over the next days Grace practises the whole sequence three times each morning. Each time it feels a little smoother, and soon she can do it without any help from Mateo.
Mateo explains what to do after an unexpected fall, in general terms. Stay calm, lie still for a moment and check for pain before trying to move, and if you are hurt, call for help.
If a person cannot get up, they should call out, or use a phone or personal alarm, and keep warm with a coat or blanket. Grace decides to keep her phone in her pocket in future.
Mateo suggests a safety plan that everyone can understand. Grace tells Anna about her exercises and agrees to phone her every morning, and Dorothy has a spare key to the house.
One morning Grace gets down to the floor and up again without any help at all. Leo, who is watching, claps his hands, and the tenth and last move is now hers.
Mateo sits down with Grace and a blank weekly calendar. He says that the next job is to fit the ten moves into a real week, without making it feel like a second job.
The plan is quite simple, and Mateo explains it step by step. Grace will walk on most days, do strength moves on two or three, and practise balance daily.
Each exercise session should begin with a short warm-up. Grace marches on the spot, swings her arms and makes easy circles with her shoulders and hips for about five minutes.
After the main exercise Grace finishes with a short cool-down. She walks slowly until her breathing returns to normal, stretches gently and drinks a glass of water.
Her finished chart goes up on the fridge door for everyone to see. She will walk on five days, do strength moves on Monday and Thursday, and balance daily, with Sunday for rest.
Rest days are an important part of the plan. The body repairs itself and grows stronger while it rests, so Grace leaves one day free between her strength sessions.
To judge how hard she is working, Mateo shows Grace a scale from one to ten. Moderate effort, like a brisk walk, is about five or six, and a hard effort is seven or eight.
Grace keeps a record of what she does, with ticks and stars on her fridge chart. Seeing the stars gather gives her a feeling of progress, and it also shows the pattern of her weeks.
Mateo says that swimming, cycling, dancing and gardening are all excellent. The ten moves are only a base, and Grace should mix them with anything that she enjoys doing.
Winter arrives, and the mornings are dark and cold. Grace stands at the window with her walking shoes in her hand, and for the first time she does not want to go out.
Grace catches a bad cold and spends a week in bed. Mateo says that resting is sensible when you are ill, and that she can return gently when she feels better.
When she feels well again, Grace goes back to short walks. She wears a hat and gloves, takes it slowly, and builds her time back up over a couple of weeks.
On icy winter mornings Grace takes extra care outside. She wears shoes with a good grip and takes short steps, and when the ice is bad she stays indoors.
Mateo explains the difference between a good ache and a warning pain. A dull tiredness in working muscles is normal, but sharp, sudden pain, or pain in a joint that lasts, is a signal to stop.

Some warning signs mean stopping at once, Mateo says. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting or sudden weakness need urgent medical help, and Mateo makes sure that Grace knows the emergency number.
Grace's knee begins to grumble, so Mateo adjusts her routine. She uses a lower step, takes shorter walks and rests more, and he says that she should see her doctor if the pain lasts.
Sleep is also an important part of recovery, Mateo says. A tired body repairs itself better with enough sleep, so some days an early night beats extra exercise.
Habits are easier if they are tied to something that you do already. Grace leaves her shoes by the door, walks after breakfast and practises her balance while the kettle boils.
On the first snowy morning Grace and Dorothy walk very carefully round Millfield Park. The trees are white and the air is clear, and winter no longer feels like an enemy.
Grace and Dorothy put a notice on the library board, and a Tuesday walking club is born. Two new friends, Ken and Priya, turn up for the very first walk.
Many people find it easier to keep exercising when they do it with others. Friends share encouragement, they notice when you are missing, and they make the miles pass much more quickly.
Anna comes to stay for the weekend and is amazed. Her mother lifts a heavy pot, goes up the stairs two at a time, and gets up from the floor without using her hands.
That evening Anna admits that she has been worried ever since the stumble. Grace tells her calmly that falls can often be prevented, and that she has never felt so sure of her own legs.
One evening Mateo tells Grace why he became a physiotherapist. As a boy he watched his grandfather lose his independence after a bad fall, and he wanted to help other families to avoid that.
Rosa asks Grace to lead the warm-up at her tai chi class. Grace is nervous, but she finds that teaching others helps her to understand each movement better herself.
At the community hall Grace visits a class where people exercise sitting on chairs. It shows her that people with limits can still move, and that a professional can adapt the exercises for them.
Dorothy spots a poster on the park fence for a five-kilometre community walk in October. It will raise money for the bandstand, and the Tuesday club decides to enter as a team.
Over the summer the club builds up, a little farther each week, from three kilometres to four and then to five. They carry water, take rests, and never push anybody to go faster than they can.
On the night before the walk, almost a year to the day after her stumble, Grace lays out her shoes and her yellow coat. She looks at the old list on the fridge, and smiles.
On the morning of the walk the park gates are crowded with walkers, balloons and music. Leo, who is five now, has a paper badge of his own and he is very proud of it.
At the starting whistle the Tuesday walkers move off together, with Grace and Dorothy at the front. They chat easily as they go, which, as Grace remarks, shows that the pace is exactly right.
The route runs down Linden Road, past the baker's and the lamp post. Grace realises that they are heading for the kerb where she tripped a year ago, and she slows down a little.
Grace steps down off the kerb and across the road, and up the opposite kerb, with a light step. Then she turns back and touches the lamp post that once saved her, and Dorothy squeezes her arm.
Grace crosses the finish line to cheers from the crowd. Leo runs beside her for the last few steps, and Anna, who has been waiting there, hugs them both and cries a little.
After the walk the whole club sits by the bandstand with tea and cake. They hear that all together the walkers have raised enough money for the first repairs, and the brass band plays.

Sitting on the grass, Mateo counts the ten moves on his fingers and reminds Grace how far she has come. She is not an athlete, he says, but she is stronger and steadier, and she has her confidence back.
That evening Grace sits down on the floor to read Leo a story, and then she stands up again without any help. Anna, who is watching from the sofa, thinks that it is a small miracle.
Priya's sister, who has come for the walk, asks Grace how she did it. Grace gives her the old envelope with the list of ten moves, and her best advice: start small, and be patient.

Walk, stand, bend, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and get up from the floor, and practise a little every day. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: Grace had spent thirty-five years in front of a classroom, and since retiring she had filled her days with the radio, the crossword and a great deal of sitting. On this grey Tuesday she was walking to the baker's at the end of Linden Road, a quiet street of terraced houses with neat front gardens. Her mind was elsewhere, running over her shopping list, her daughter's telephone call and the roof tiles that needed mending.

It happened in less than a second: her toe caught the lip of the kerb, her weight tipped forward, and the pavement seemed to leap up towards her face. Her hands, which should have flown out to save her, stayed pinned uselessly at her sides. Time stretched and slowed, and she heard herself gasp as though the sound belonged to somebody else.

A stranger in a green coat, who had been walking behind her, darted forward and caught her by the elbow, and she flung her free hand around a cold lamp post. For a few seconds the two of them stood there in silence while she waited for the pain to arrive. It never came, and when she checked her knees and wrists she found nothing damaged except her dignity.

Grace thanked her rescuer several times, far more warmly than the moment required, and then turned back towards home without so much as a glance at the baker's shop. Her heart was hammering against her ribs and her knees had the unreliable feel of wet paper. The street that she had walked a thousand times now looked like a place full of hidden traps.

In her small kitchen she made a pot of tea and sat down with it, noticing that her hands trembled a little as she raised the cup. The shaking brought back a memory she had spent years avoiding: her mother, who had fallen on a wet step at the age of eighty and never walked properly again. Grace had always told herself, without ever quite believing it, that such things happened only to other people.

As the tea cooled, Grace made an honest inventory of her week and was dismayed by what she found. Since retiring she had walked from the front door to the car, from the car to the shop and from the shop to the sofa, and almost nowhere else. For decades her work had kept her on her feet all day, and without noticing she had swapped movement for comfort.

The next morning the sun came out, and Grace wandered into the garden mainly to avoid thinking. On the other side of the low fence her neighbour Mateo, a calm man in his forties, was hanging washing on a line and humming to himself. He glanced over, smiled and asked how she was, and to her surprise she found that the question made her eyes sting.

It all came out in a rush: the kerb, the stranger, the lamp post, and the dreadful thought of her mother's broken hip. Mateo did not interrupt, and when she had finished he nodded slowly and said that he worked as a physiotherapist and had heard many stories like hers. He did not say that she was foolish to be frightened, and Grace felt grateful for that.

Mateo explained that almost everyone trips now and then, but that serious falls are not an unavoidable price of growing older. The human body, he said, is built to move, and it tends to stay capable of movement for as long as it is asked to do so. What changes with age, he added, is often less about years than about habits, and habits can be changed.

Before she could lose her nerve, Grace asked whether he might be willing to show her how to look after her body, and Mateo agreed at once with an easy smile. He suggested that they begin on Saturday morning, over a cup of tea, but he asked for one promise first. She was to tell her doctor about her plans, because a sensible start, he said, is a safe start.

On Saturday morning Mateo appeared at the garden gate with a battered notebook, a pencil behind his ear and two steaming mugs of coffee. He settled into a chair at the little table and asked Grace to describe an ordinary day, starting from the moment she woke up. It was not an examination, he promised, but a way of finding out where they were beginning.

Grace counted on her fingers as she described her routine: breakfast at the table, the radio in the armchair, a short drive, the crossword, the television in the evening. Mateo wrote quietly while she talked, and when she reached the end they added up the hours together. The total, nearly ten hours of sitting, was far larger than either of them had expected.

Mateo explained that large studies have linked long hours of unbroken sitting with a higher risk of several health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Researchers cannot prove that sitting alone is to blame, since people who sit a lot often do less of other healthy things too. Still, he said, the advice is simple and cheap: stand up, stretch and walk about every half an hour or so.

Mateo turned a page and drew a heart, a bed and a smiling face, and explained that people who are regularly active tend to enjoy a healthier heart, stronger bones and muscles, and often better sleep and mood. The size of the benefit varies from person to person, he cautioned, and nobody can promise a particular result. On average, though, the evidence for the benefits of regular movement is among the strongest in all of medicine.

Mateo drew a calendar and explained that official health guidelines, such as those from the World Health Organization, suggest that adults aim for roughly 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity every week. They also recommend exercises that strengthen the muscles on two or more days of the week, to keep the body capable as well as busy. He stressed that these numbers are targets to grow towards and not a test to pass, and that any movement at all is better than none.

For people over sixty-five, Mateo went on, the guidelines add a third ingredient, which is balance training, usually recommended on about three days a week alongside strength work. Balance and strength together are among the best defences we have against falls, and the encouraging news is that both can be improved at almost any age. Grace, who had feared that her stumble was simply the beginning of the end, felt something loosen in her chest.

Then Mateo told her his big idea, which was that nearly everything a person does in a day, from carrying shopping to getting off the floor, is built from about ten basic movements. If those ten stay in good working order, he said, ordinary life stays easy, and if they fade, even small tasks begin to feel like obstacles. He did not claim that it was a perfect scheme, only a useful way to think about a body.

He read the list aloud, slowly, while Grace copied it onto the back of an envelope: walk, sit to stand, hinge, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and, last of all, the floor. A few of the words puzzled her, but Mateo promised that each would be explained in turn, one at a time, with nothing rushed. She stuck the envelope to the fridge door with a magnet shaped like a strawberry.

On Monday Grace kept an appointment with Dr Okafor, a brisk and kindly woman who listened to the whole story without checking her watch. She measured Grace's blood pressure, asked about her health and her medicines, and said that regular movement was an excellent idea provided that she built up gradually. Grace left with a lighter step, and with the pleasing feeling of having been given permission.

That evening Mateo leaned on the fence and gave Grace his three golden rules, counting them off on his fingers. First, begin smaller than you think you should; second, be regular rather than heroic; third, stop whenever there is sharp pain, because discomfort and damage are not the same thing. Tomorrow, he said, they would start with the oldest and best of the ten moves, which was simply walking.

Early on Monday morning, with the dew still on the front gardens, Grace tied her shoes at the door while Mateo waited on the path. The first of the ten moves, he announced, was the oldest and simplest of them all, and every other move rests on it. It was just walking, but he promised to show her how to do it better.

Walking, Mateo pointed out, costs nothing, needs no equipment and can be done almost anywhere, and yet it works the legs, the heart, the lungs and the sense of balance all at once. It is the foundation on which the other nine moves are built, and for most people it is the best possible place to begin. Many people, he added, forget how good it is because it is so ordinary.

Mateo glanced at her feet and pronounced her old shoes perfectly acceptable, since they were comfortable, supportive and not yet worn through at the heel. He explained that a good walking shoe has a firm, flexible sole and enough room for the toes, and that price is a poor guide to quality. The best shoe, he said, is the one that feels good and that you will actually wear.

Mateo showed her how to walk with a little more care than she was used to, looking ahead rather than at her feet, with her shoulders loose and her arms swinging gently. Each step, he said, should land on the heel and roll smoothly forward onto the toes, with the stride a comfortable length rather than a long, straining one. Good posture, he added, is simply the body stacked up neatly, with no need for stiffness.

How fast should she actually go, Grace wanted to know, and where was the line between brisk and breathless. Mateo introduced the talk test, a rough but reliable guide to moderate effort: at a brisk pace your breathing quickens and you feel warmer, yet you can still speak in full sentences, although you could not sing a song. If she could not talk at all, he said, she was going too fast, and if she could sing, she was going too slowly.

They set off together, down Linden Road to the corner and back again, which took barely ten minutes. By the time they reached her gate Grace was breathing hard and her calves were complaining, and she was astonished that a stroll she had once taken without noticing now felt like a small expedition. Mateo congratulated her warmly, because a start, he said, is the hardest part of any journey.

Walking, Grace discovered, is a very different way of seeing a street from driving along it. She noticed the cherry tree turning yellow at number eight, a cat dozing on a wall, and the warm smell drifting from the baker's open door, none of which she had registered in twenty years. The slower pace had given her back a neighbourhood she had somehow stopped noticing.

Mateo's advice for the weeks ahead was gloriously dull: walk for ten minutes every day, then add a minute or two each week as it begins to feel easy. Bodies adapt gradually, he said, and the tendons and joints take longer to adjust than the muscles do, so patience is part of the training. A walker who does too much too soon, he warned, is usually a walker who stops.

By the end of the first week Grace had walked on six mornings out of seven, and her legs ached in a dull, slightly pleasant way, like an engine that has been started after a long winter. Mateo told her that such tiredness was entirely normal and usually faded within a few days, whereas sharp or lasting pain was a signal to stop and to seek advice. She was, she realised with some amusement, rather proud of her sore legs and of what they stood for.

Two weeks in, Grace noticed a change that she had not expected and could not quite explain: she felt lighter in her mood, and she was sleeping more deeply than she had for years. Mateo said that many people report this, and that studies do suggest regular walking can lift the spirits and help sleep, though the effect differs from one person to the next. Whatever the reason might be, she was not about to argue with such a welcome gift.

By the third week the corner of Linden Road was no longer far enough for Grace, and her morning route had stretched to twenty minutes. She now walked past the baker's, round the church and through the tall green gates of Millfield Park, where the paths were lined with chestnut trees. Each day she added a little more, and each day the park felt a little nearer.

Dorothy, who lived at number twelve and had views on most subjects, spotted Grace marching past the bowling green and announced that she would come too. They talked without pause for the whole circuit, and Grace explained, with a certain pride, that being able to chat was precisely the sign of a comfortable brisk pace. Dorothy, slightly out of breath, said that she hoped it was also the sign of a good cake afterwards.

Mateo then introduced an idea he called intervals, which meant alternating a minute of faster walking with a minute at an easy pace, and repeating the pattern several times. The fast minutes, he explained, nudge the heart and lungs a little harder, while the slow ones give the body time to recover, and many people find that it makes a walk fly by. He suggested that she try it twice a week and see how it felt.

On the far side of Millfield Park rose a gentle grassy hill that Grace had always walked around, and one morning she decided to walk up it instead. Her heart thumped and her thighs burned, and Mateo, when she told him, was delighted, because slopes make the legs and the heart work harder at no extra cost. Even a modest hill, he said, is a free gift to anyone who is willing to take it.

One morning the rain came down in grey sheets, and for a moment Grace stood at the window and considered staying in. Instead she put on a bright yellow coat, which made her easy to see, and walked her usual route with extra care on the wet leaves and slippery paving. She came home soaked, cheerful and ten minutes better off, and she wondered why she had hesitated.

Dorothy proudly produced a pedometer, a small device that counts steps, and asked Mateo whether ten thousand steps a day was really the goal.
