He replied that the figure began as a slogan rather than as a scientific finding, and that studies suggest the benefits for many adults rise until about seven or eight thousand steps a day and then level off. There is no magic number, he said, and the best target is a little more than you do now.

Mateo told her that regular brisk walking has been linked in many studies with a lower risk of heart disease, because the heart is a muscle and, like any muscle, it grows stronger when it is used. He added a note of caution, however, that walking works best as part of a healthy way of living, and that no study can promise an outcome to any single person. Grace, who thought of her own heart rather fondly now, promised to keep it busy.

Grace had begun, to her surprise, to look forward to her walks, and the park in particular. Studies suggest that time outdoors in daylight, especially among trees and grass, tends to lift people's mood and ease their worries, and she certainly felt calmer sitting on the bench at the top of the hill. She stayed there for a few minutes each morning, watching the leaves, before turning for home.

Inevitably there came a morning when Grace did not want to go, when the sofa was warm, the sky was dull and her legs felt like lead. Mateo had warned her about such days and had a remedy, which he called the two-minute rule: put on your shoes, step outside and walk for two minutes, and then you may go home if you still wish. She did not go home, of course, because the hardest part was already behind her.

A month after the stumble, Grace walked for half an hour without stopping, brisk and upright, and the notebook in her pocket was crowded with ticks. She felt a quiet happiness that she could not remember feeling in years, a feeling of having taken a small but real step back towards herself. Mateo, leaning on the fence that evening, said that the first move was safely in place and that it was time to meet the second.

The following Saturday Mateo carried a plain wooden chair into the middle of Grace's kitchen and invited her to look at it as though it were a piece of gym equipment. The second move, he said, was one that she performed thousands of times a year without a thought, which was standing up from a seat. It sounded simple, but he assured her that it was one of the most important movements a body can make.

Sit to stand, Mateo explained, is a squat in disguise, a movement we repeat from armchairs, car seats, benches and toilets dozens of times a day. People who lose the strength to do it without help often lose a good deal of independence with it, which is why physiotherapists pay it so much attention. Grace looked down at the plain wooden chair in front of her with a good deal more respect than before.

The set-up, Mateo said, matters more than anything else, and he moved her feet into place with a gentle tap of his fingers. She was to sit near the front edge of a firm chair, with her feet flat on the floor, roughly hip-width apart and tucked back slightly beneath her knees. A wall behind the chair, he added, would stop it from sliding away, and she should never use a chair on wheels.

From there, said Mateo, you lean forward from the hips until your nose is roughly above your toes, because this brings your weight over your feet. Then you push down through them as though you were trying to press the floor away, and you rise until you are standing tall, with your hips fully open. Grace tried it and felt her thighs and buttocks working together, a sensation she had almost forgotten.

Mateo then pointed out that the way down matters as much as the way up, and that many of us simply collapse into our chairs without control. Grace was to push her hips backwards, bend her knees and lower herself in a slow, steady glide until she touched the seat. The controlled descent, he said, is a surprisingly good exercise in itself, because the muscles work hard while they are lengthening.

On her first attempts Grace pressed hard on her knees and on the seat to haul herself upright, and she apologised to Mateo for cheating. He laughed and told her that there was nothing wrong with using her arms to begin with, since every exercise should start at a level you can manage. As her legs grew stronger, he said, she could rely on her hands a little less each week.

Mateo took out his phone and described a test that therapists often use, in which a person stands up from a chair as many times as possible in thirty seconds, with the arms folded across the chest. The number you reach, he said, can be compared with typical results for your age, but it is only a rough guide and says little about your worth as a human being. Its real value is as a starting line, something to improve upon in a month's time.

Mateo started the timer, and Grace rose and sat, rose and sat, counting breathlessly under her breath until he called time. Nine, she reported, and he wrote the number in the notebook without comment, as a measurement and not a verdict. They would try the test again in a month, he said, and she was surprised at how much she wanted to beat nine.

Mateo's most practical suggestion was to hide the exercise inside ordinary life: every time she rose from a chair she should do it deliberately, slowly and without leaning on her hands if she could. She could also stand and sit a few times during each television advertisement, he said, which would give her several sets of practice before the programme even resumed. Habits, he reminded her with a smile, are always built from small things done often and without fuss.

Dorothy arrived for tea, heard all about the chair and insisted on a turn herself, declaring that she could do it in her sleep. Within six stands her thighs were trembling and she was laughing so much that she had to sit down, and Mateo told her cheerfully that the trembling is simply the muscles working hard. She then demanded a go at the thirty-second test, and Grace was pleased to discover that her friend scored only eight.

Mateo drew a quick sketch of a standing figure and shaded in the thighs and buttocks, which are the largest muscles in the human body. These muscles, he said, do the heavy lifting whenever we rise, walk, climb or step over an obstacle, and so keeping them strong repays the effort many times over. The glutes and quadriceps, as they are called, are quite literally the engine room of everyday life.

Muscle, Mateo explained, tends to shrink gradually from middle age onwards, particularly in people who do little strenuous activity, and this loss can quietly erode strength and balance. The good news is that muscle responds to training at any stage of life, and studies have shown real gains in people in their eighties and nineties. It is never too late to ask a muscle to grow, he said, but it does have to be asked.

Once the basic move felt easy, Mateo showed Grace how to make it more demanding without adding any equipment at all, simply by slowing down the descent. She was to count to three while she lowered herself into the chair, resisting gravity all the way, and she was to feel the muscles of her thighs working harder than before. The burn in her legs, he told her cheerfully, was the sensation of progress.

A further step, said Mateo, was to hold some weight against the chest, and the cupboard supplied a two-kilogram bag of rice that was just right. Grace clasped it to her front and rose from the chair, and she felt immediately how much more the legs and the stomach muscles had to do. A bag of rice was, she remarked, the cheapest piece of gym equipment she had ever bought.

Strength work, Mateo told her, is a rather different thing from walking, because the muscles do not grow during the exercise but afterwards, while they rest and repair. Two or three sessions a week, with a day off in between, is enough for most people, and more is not necessarily better. Grace, who had been planning to do it every morning, was relieved to be allowed a holiday.

Mateo introduced a pair of terms that every gym user knows: a repetition is one complete movement, and a set is a group of repetitions done in a row. A sensible target, he said, was eight to twelve repetitions per set, ending when the muscles felt tired but the movement was still smooth and under control. If her form began to collapse, she should stop, since a sloppy repetition teaches the body very little.

The morning after her first proper leg session Grace found that her thighs protested loudly on the stairs, and she descended them like a woman of ninety. Mateo, unmoved, told her that such delayed soreness is common after unfamiliar exercise and usually fades in two or three days, whereas sharp pain, swelling or an ache that lingers deserves attention. A gentle walk, he added kindly, often makes stiff and tired muscles feel a good deal better than resting does.

Mateo added that the benefits of exercise were not confined to the muscles, since bone is living tissue that responds to the loads placed on it. Walking, climbing and strength training all appear to help the skeleton hold on to its density, which matters because weak bones are the reason that so many falls end in fractures. Anyone worried about bone health, he said, should ask a doctor, who can arrange tests and offer proper advice.

Exercise alone is not enough, Mateo went on, because the muscles need raw materials to repair themselves, and among these is protein, found in foods such as eggs, fish, beans, dairy and meat. He was careful to add that individual needs vary with health, size and medication, and that a dietitian is the right person to ask about a personal plan. He was only a physiotherapist, he reminded her with a shrug, and not a nutrition expert of any kind.

A month after the first test Mateo set the stopwatch going again, and Grace rose and sat with her arms folded across her chest, counting under her breath. Twelve, he announced when the time was up, three more than the first attempt, and she had not touched her knees once. She was surprised to find that her eyes were prickling with tears, because the number represented something much bigger than the chair.

One breezy afternoon Grace swooped down to pick up a heavy basket of wet washing, and a sharp twinge shot across her lower back. It passed within seconds, but Mateo, who had been watching over the fence, hurried round and said that the moment had come for the third move. It was called the hinge, he said, and it was the secret of bending without complaint.

Mateo called the third move the hinge, because it works like a door swinging on its hinge: the body folds forward at the hips while the back stays long and calm. The great muscles of the buttocks and the backs of the thighs, which are built for heavy work, then take the load instead of the smaller and more delicate muscles of the lower back. Every time we pick something up, he said, we can choose which muscles will do the job.

To feel the movement, Mateo said, stand with the feet about hip-width apart and rest the hands on the tops of the thighs. Then push the hips backwards, as though you were trying to close a car door with your bottom, letting the knees soften and the hands slide towards the knees while the chest tips forward. Grace giggled at the image, but she felt the backs of her legs stretch and engage.

Mateo handed her a broom handle and asked her to hold it against her back, so that it touched her head, the middle of her upper back and the base of her spine. If all three contact points stayed in place as she hinged forward, he explained, then her back was staying long and steady while her hips did the real work. It was a humble tool, but the feedback it gave her was remarkably honest, and it never once flattered her technique.

Mateo was keen to avoid frightening her, so he explained that bending with a rounded back is not automatically dangerous, since the human spine is a good deal tougher and more adaptable than most of us believe. The hinge, he said, was not a rule that must never be broken but a strong and efficient habit, and one that spares the back when loads are heavy or the body is tired. Most people, he added with a reassuring smile, can pick up the movement in a single afternoon of patient practice.

Over the next few days Grace practised the hinge wherever she could, taking a pan from the lowest kitchen shelf, putting on her shoes and picking up post from the mat. Awkward at first, the movement soon began to feel natural, and she noticed with satisfaction that the grumbling in her lower back had faded to nothing. Her thighs, she noted wryly, were now doing jobs that her back had been doing for years.

Lifting an object off the ground, Mateo explained, is the hinge put to work, and a few simple habits make it safer: keep the load close to the body, because distance makes it harder to control, and breathe steadily. Then stand up by driving through the legs and hips, and above all avoid twisting while the weight is in your hands. Grace used the method on a sack of compost and was astonished by how light it felt.

The garden became Grace's practice ground, where she hinged to weed, to plant bulbs and to shift heavy pots from the path. Mateo told her that there was no shame in kneeling on a foam mat or perching on a low stool when her body asked for a change, since variety is kinder to the body than any single position. Gardening, he said, is a fine form of exercise, and she had been doing it for forty years without knowing.

Grace asked about her back, and Mateo said that back pain is extraordinarily common, affecting most people at some point, and that the great majority of episodes settle down within a few weeks. Staying gently active generally helps more than lying in bed, although severe pain, numbness, weakness in a leg or problems with the bladder or bowel need medical attention without delay. Her twinge, he said reassuringly, sounded like an ordinary strain, but he was not a doctor and could not diagnose it.

A week afterwards Grace faced the same wicker basket of wet washing, and this time she was ready for it. She set her feet, pushed her hips back, hugged the basket close to her chest and rose in a single smooth motion without the slightest twinge. Mateo, watching from the fence with a mug in his hand, gave her a small round of applause.

As the autumn weather turned damp, Grace's front door began to stick in its frame, and she had to put her shoulder to it every time she came home. Mateo, passing on the pavement, said that she had just demonstrated the fourth move, which was the push. It covers any movement in which we press something away from us, from opening a heavy door to getting up off the floor.

We push far more often than we notice, said Mateo, whether we are opening a door, shunting a supermarket trolley, easing a pram along a pavement or levering ourselves up from the floor. All of these actions ask the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms to drive forward together, helped by the legs and the muscles of the trunk. A person who pushes well, he said, is a person who is rarely defeated by an everyday object.

The gentlest kind of press-up, Mateo said, is performed standing up against a wall. Grace placed her palms flat at shoulder height, stepped back until her arms were fully extended, and kept her feet on the floor with her body leaning forward in a straight line. It looked easy, but she knew by now that he never offered anything that was truly effortless.

Grace bent her elbows and let her chest drift towards the wall, then pressed back until her arms were straight again. Mateo reminded her to breathe out as she pushed away and to keep her body in one long line from her head to her heels, without letting her hips sag or stick out behind. By the tenth repetition her shoulders were warm and her arms were quietly complaining.

Once the wall felt easy, Mateo showed her how to progress by moving her hands to a lower surface, first the kitchen counter, then a sturdy table, then the seat of a chair. The lower the surface, he said, the greater the share of body weight that the arms have to push, so the exercise grows harder by degrees without any extra equipment. Only much later, if she wished and if her shoulders and wrists agreed, would she need to think about trying the floor.

A good push, Mateo told her, is a whole-body event: the chest and shoulders drive the movement, the backs of the arms straighten the elbows, and the stomach muscles keep the body from sagging. That is why the humble press-up has survived for generations in every kind of training. It teaches the body to work as a single, well-organised unit, which is exactly what ordinary life demands of it.

Mateo then moved on to the overhead push, which is what happens whenever we lift a tin or a casserole dish onto a high shelf. He advised her to use a light weight at first, to keep her ribs tucked down instead of arching her back, and to press upwards in a smooth line close to her ears. If she had ever felt pain in the shoulders, he added, she should go gently and ask a professional for advice.

Grace began to see pushing movements everywhere: the heavy shop door, the trolley piled with a week's food and the old mower she steered across the lawn on dry Sundays. All of them, Mateo pointed out, used exactly the muscles she was training, so the exercises were not an artificial chore but rehearsals for life. Everything she lifted or shoved in the course of a day, he said, was a small bonus.

One morning Grace felt a pinching sensation at the front of her shoulder as she pushed, and she wondered whether she ought to carry on. Mateo told her firmly that a mild effort or burning in the muscle is fine, but a sharp or pinching pain in a joint is a signal to stop and to seek a professional opinion. Pushing through real pain, he said, is bravery of entirely the wrong sort, and it is the quickest way to end a promising habit.

By the end of the week Grace could manage fifteen wall press-ups in a row, and she wrote the number proudly in her notebook beside a small star. Her grandson Leo, who was four and who had come to stay for the afternoon, copied her at once, pressing against the living-room wall with a ferocious frown. They counted together, and he announced to everybody that his grandmother was very strong.

On a wet Thursday Grace and Mateo went to the shops together, and the heavy glass door of the pharmacy refused to open until she hauled on it with both hands. Mateo, waiting behind her with the umbrella, said that she had just given him the perfect example of the fifth move, which was the pull. It was the natural partner of the push, he said, and quite as important.

Pulling, Mateo explained as they waited in the pharmacy queue, covers any movement in which we draw something towards our bodies, such as opening a heavy door, hauling on a rope or starting the engine of a lawnmower. It relies mainly on the muscles of the upper back and the fronts of the arms. Most of us, he said with some certainty, do far more pushing than pulling in the course of a normal week.

Mateo remarked that a great many people spend hours each day hunched towards a desk, a phone or a steering wheel, with their shoulders curled forward and their heads poked out in front. A strong upper back can make it easier to sit and stand comfortably, he said, although there is no single perfect posture, and the best position is always the next one. Pulling exercises, in other words, are a gentle counterbalance to the way that modern life bends us forward.

Mateo brought round a long rubber exercise band, looped it safely around the handle of the kitchen door and put the ends into Grace's hands. She stepped back until the band was taut, then pulled her elbows behind her and gently squeezed her shoulder blades together as if she were holding a pencil between them. It felt oddly satisfying, as though a drawer in her back had been opened that had been stuck for years.

A second version of the pull, Mateo said, needed nothing more than a bag of shopping and a chair. Grace rested one hand on the chair, bent forward with a long back, let the bag hang below her shoulder and pulled it up towards her ribs, lowering it again under control before she changed sides. Her friends at the bowling club, she suspected, would be astonished to hear that she was rowing in her kitchen.

As with every other move, Grace found that her whole day was full of pulling once she knew how to look for it. She tugged weeds out of damp earth, drew the washing line towards her peg by peg, wrestled with a swollen drawer and hauled a heavy bag from the boot of Dorothy's car. Each of these small acts, Mateo reassured her, was a bit of free training for the back.

A good rule of thumb, Mateo said, is to balance every pushing exercise with a pulling one, so that the muscles at the front and back of the shoulders are trained evenly. The idea is not that any imbalance spells disaster, he added, but that a body developed in one direction only tends to feel lopsided over time. Grace made a note to match her wall press-ups with an equal number of rows.

Dorothy, who had spent forty years bent over a sewing machine and whose shoulders had curled forward to match, demanded a turn with the rubber band. She found it a great deal harder than she had expected, and her face went pink with the effort, while Grace tried very hard not to look smug. Mateo adjusted the band to an easier tension and promised her that the first week is always the worst.

A few weeks into the rowing, Grace caught sight of herself in the hall mirror and saw a woman who was standing noticeably taller, with her shoulders open and her chin level. Mateo, to whom she reported this, pointed out cautiously that posture depends on many things and that the band could not take all the credit. Grace, however, was not remotely interested in being modest about it, and she stood a little taller still.

That Sunday afternoon Mateo counted off the moves on his fingers and discovered that Grace had now met five of the ten: walking, sitting and standing, the hinge, the push and the pull. This, he declared, called for a celebration, and the two of them took lemon cake and tea into the garden, where the late sun lay across the flower beds. Half the journey was complete, and Grace was no longer afraid of the other half.

On the way back from the Saturday market Grace staggered up Linden Road with a bag in each hand, her arms burning and her fingers numb. Mateo, who met her at the gate and took one of the bags without being asked, said that she had been practising the sixth move, which was the carry. It was, he said with a rueful smile, the move that most of us do worst and notice least.

Carrying, Mateo explained, is the marriage of two earlier moves, since it begins with a hinge and a lift and continues with a walk. It covers shopping, suitcases, baskets of washing, toolboxes and, most precious of all, small grandchildren, and every one of these loads asks the grip, the shoulders and the whole trunk to work together. A strong carry, he said, is what lets people stay useful to the ones they love.

Mateo's favourite exercise for the carry was so simple that Grace thought he was joking: she was to pick up a weight in each hand, stand tall with her shoulders relaxed and walk briskly in short, steady steps. She filled two watering cans from the tap and set off across the lawn, feeling her stomach muscles tighten and her grip work to hold the handles. By the time she reached the far fence her forearms were warm and her shoulders were pleasantly tired.

Grip strength, Mateo told her, has been studied surprisingly often, and large studies have linked a firm grip with better health and longer life in older adults. That does not prove that the grip itself is the cause, since a strong hand may simply reflect a body that is strong and active everywhere else. Still, he said, it is a pleasant habit to be able to open a jar without help.

As with all the other moves, he insisted that the sensible way to start was small: two full bottles of water carried to the garden gate and back, with the shoulders level and the stomach gently braced. When that felt easy she might carry a little farther or choose a heavier load, adding only one thing at a time, so that she could always tell what her body liked. Progress, he said, is built on patience and small steps, and never on heroic and foolish leaps.

A single heavy bag, Mateo explained, is a different challenge from two, because it tries to pull the body sideways, and the muscles of the trunk must resist the lean in order to keep her upright. He advised her to carry on one side for a short distance, to keep her shoulders level and then to swap hands, so that both sides received equal training. The famous suitcase carry, he added, is one of the best exercises for the waist ever invented.

When Anna brought Leo round for tea the little boy ran up the path with his arms raised, shouting for a lift, and Grace realised that this was exactly the moment she had been preparing for. She hinged at the hips, scooped him up and hugged him close to her chest, then rose through her legs with her back long and her grip firm. Leo, who weighed about as much as a sack of potatoes, giggled with delight, and she felt entirely safe.

The practical lessons arrived one after another, and Grace began to pack her shopping into two smaller bags of roughly equal weight, rather than into one dreadful one that dragged her sideways. She put the heavy tins low and the bread on top, and she took a rest at the half-way bench whenever her fingers began to tingle. Nobody, she decided as she sat down, could possibly be too proud or too fit to need a rest now and then.

For longer trips Mateo recommended a sturdy rucksack worn on both shoulders, since it keeps the load close to the spine and spreads the weight across the strongest parts of the body. Grace bought a small blue one, and she was amazed at how much lighter the weekly shop felt when it rode on her back. It also left both her hands free, she noticed, which might matter a great deal on any day when she stumbled.

At the end of the month Grace carried two full watering cans from one end of the garden to the other and back again without stopping, with her shoulders level and her head high. Dorothy, who had been watching from a deckchair with a cup of tea, applauded loudly, and Mateo ticked off the sixth move in his notebook. More than half of the journey now lay behind her, and the other half looked almost welcoming.

One damp afternoon Grace paused at the foot of her own staircase, which she had climbed twice a day for thirty years, and found herself studying it as though it were a mountain. Mateo, who had come in to return a borrowed book, followed her gaze and said that the seventh move was climbing. It included stairs, steps and slopes, he said, and it asked more of the heart than any other move so far.

Climbing, Mateo said, is not only about mountains: it includes stairs, steps, kerbs, ramps and slopes, in short anything that asks the body to lift itself upwards against gravity. That extra effort makes the legs work harder and raises the heart rate more quickly than walking on the flat, which is why a flight of stairs can leave a beginner breathless. Breathlessness, he added with a smile, is simply an honest and rather useful measurement of how fit you are today.

Before any practice began, Mateo inspected the staircase with the thoroughness of a safety officer. He tested the handrail, switched the landing light on and off, picked a stray book from the third step and frowned at Grace's loose slippers, since a bright, clear stair is the first condition of confident climbing. Grace did not argue with him at all, because she had grown rather fond of his fussing.

The exercise that Mateo proposed was the step-up, which he said was the staircase in miniature: place a whole foot on the bottom stair, press through it until you stand upright, then step down gently, controlling the descent. After ten steps she was to change the leading foot and repeat, always with one hand lightly on the rail. It was a very small exercise, but her thighs reported on it in loud detail.

Mateo told her that a number of recent studies have found that short bursts of stair climbing, scattered through the day, can improve fitness in people who do not otherwise exercise much. Although more research is needed, he said, it is an encouraging idea for anyone who owns a staircase. Grace resolved to treat every single journey to the bedroom as a tiny and worthwhile workout.

Coming down proved to be a different challenge, as Mateo had warned, because the legs must act as brakes and the muscles are working while they lengthen, which is both tiring and slightly risky. Grace descended with a hand on the rail, placing the whole of each foot on the stair and looking carefully at where she was going. She was not to hurry, he said, and never to carry a load that blocked her view of the steps.

After the third day of step-ups Grace's knees began to feel stiff and slightly sore, and she asked whether she should be worried. Mateo said that strong thighs often protect the knees, and that many people find their joints feel better once the muscles around them grow stronger. Pain which is sharp, swollen or lasting, however, should be examined by a doctor or a physiotherapist, and he was only a neighbour, he reminded her, and not a diagnosis.

On Sunday they walked up the long hill in Millfield Park, and Mateo showed Grace how to deal with it, using shorter steps, a slight lean from the ankles and arms swinging in a steady rhythm. The hill grew less steep as her breathing settled, and at the top she found that she was laughing. A slope that had once seemed an enemy had become something much closer to a friend.

The talk test, Mateo reminded her, applies on slopes and stairs as well as on the flat: breathing hard is normal, but if you feel faint, dizzy or tight in the chest, you must stop and rest. If those feelings return or do not settle, he added, she should speak to a doctor promptly. Fitness is built on effort that is firm but never frightening, he told her, and it is always worth listening to the body.

At the top of the hill Grace turned round and looked down over the rooftops, the church tower and the green blur of the park, with the wind in her hair and her heart beating steadily. Seven of the ten moves now belonged to her, and she felt as though she had climbed a great deal more than a hill. Mateo, arriving a few steps behind her, was not even slightly breathless, but he pretended to be.

One cold morning Grace tried to reverse her little car out of the drive and discovered that she could hardly turn her head and shoulders far enough to see behind her. She managed in the end, but she was flustered, and she told Mateo about it later over the fence. The eighth move, he said, was exactly the one she had been missing, and it was called the twist.

A twist, Mateo said, is a turn of the upper body over the hips, and we use it constantly without realising, whether looking behind us at a crossing, reaching for a seat belt or throwing a ball for a dog. The spine is designed to rotate, mostly in the middle of the back, but like any joint it becomes stiff when it is not asked to move. Stiffness, he told her, is usually a habit long before it ever becomes a medical condition, and habits can be changed.

The seated twist was the first exercise Mateo taught her: sit tall on the front of a chair, fold the arms across the chest and slowly turn the upper body to look over one shoulder, then the other. She was to turn smoothly, without jerking, and to breathe out as she went round. It was so gentle that Grace doubted it could do any good, until she tried it ten times and felt her ribs begin to loosen.

Mateo emphasised that the twist should come mostly from the chest and the upper back, with the hips and knees staying quiet, because the lower back is built for far less rotation than the middle of the spine. A gentle stretch is plenty, he said, and one should never force the movement or bounce at the end of the range. If it hurts, she was to stop, and not to take it as a challenge.

To make the twist a little more demanding, Mateo gave her a light bag of rice to hold at chest height and asked her to stand with her feet apart and turn slowly from one side to the other. She was to keep her hips facing forward and to let the movement come from the middle of the body, breathing out as she turned. By the tenth turn she could feel muscles in her sides that she had not known she possessed.

Mateo explained that the muscles around the middle of the body, the so-called core, have two jobs: they turn the trunk when we want to twist, and they resist unwanted twisting when we carry a load on one side. In a sense, he said, the core is less a set of muscles than a team that works together to protect the spine. Grace recalled the suitcase carry and understood at last why it had made her sides ache.

After a brisk walk, with her muscles warm, Grace learned a handful of gentle stretches for her calves, thighs, chest and back, each held for about thirty seconds until she felt a mild pull. Mateo said that flexibility is one of the pleasures of a body that has been looked after, and that a stretch should feel like a long sigh rather than a battle. She should never bounce, he said firmly, and she should never push into sharp discomfort for the sake of reaching a little farther.

Dorothy wanted to know whether stretching would stop her from hurting herself, and Mateo gave the honest answer, which was that the research is mixed and the experts do not entirely agree. It does not seem to protect everyone from injury, he said, but it can help many people feel looser, and it is pleasant, so there is no good reason to give it up. He was not in the business, he added, of promising what science cannot prove.

On Saturday afternoon Dorothy dragged Grace to a tea dance at the community hall, where couples of every age were gliding round the floor to a scratchy record of a waltz. The steps and turns, Mateo said when he heard about it, were wonderful for twisting, balance and spirits all at once, and nobody would ever call dancing a chore. Grace had been out of practice for decades, but she stepped on her partner's toes only twice.

A month after the awkward morning Grace backed her little car out of the drive in a single smooth movement, turning her head and shoulders far enough to see the whole of the road behind her. There was no crick in her neck and no flustered fumbling, and she was sure that she looked rather competent. She gave the horn a modest toot as she passed Mateo's house, and he waved from his upstairs window.

The ninth move, Mateo announced, was balance, and he began with a trick so ordinary that Grace thought he was teasing her: stand on one leg while you brush your teeth, holding the sink if you need to. Two minutes of tooth-brushing twice a day, he pointed out, would give her four minutes of practice without a single minute taken from her schedule. It was, he said with a grin, quite possibly the cheapest training programme in the whole world, and the dullest.

Balance, Mateo explained, is not a single skill but a collaboration between the eyes, the inner ear and the sensors in the feet and joints, whose messages the brain combines every second without our noticing. When any of these partners grows weaker, the others can compensate, but only if they are exercised. Balance, in other words, is very much a use-it-or-lose-it ability, and the sooner we practise it the better.

Balance does tend to decline with age, Mateo said, but much of the loss comes from disuse and not from the passing of years, and training can win much of it back. Studies of older adults have shown measurable improvements within a few weeks of regular practice, and some people are astonished at how quickly it returns. Grace, who had wondered whether her best days were behind her, found this the most encouraging news of all.

Mateo took her into the kitchen and explained how to begin safely: stand beside the counter with one hand resting on it, lift one foot a few centimetres from the floor and hold it there for a count of ten. Then she was to change legs, and repeat the exercise several times, keeping a firm surface close in case she wobbled. A wobble, he reminded her, is not a failure, because it is the body learning.

Grace practised every morning, and after a week she needed just a single finger on the counter, and a week after that she let go altogether and stood like a heron. Mateo told her that she could make the exercise gradually harder by holding it for longer, by standing on a folded towel or by turning her head from side to side, but only with something sturdy within reach. Safety came first, he said, and ambition a distant second, and she should never practise on slippery floors or in bare feet on stairs.

Heel-to-toe walking, said Mateo, is an exercise that circus performers would recognise: you place the heel of one foot directly in front of the toes of the other, as though crossing a tightrope. Grace tried it in the hallway with a hand trailing along the wall for safety, and she was surprised at how much concentration it took. She wobbled a good deal on the first day, but by the end of the week she could walk from one end to the other.

Balance can be trained outdoors as well, Mateo said, and the park was a splendid gymnasium: walking on soft grass, turning the head to look about, stepping over fallen branches and wandering along gently uneven paths. Each of these ordinary challenges asked the brain and the feet to cooperate, and he suggested that she do them on days when she felt steady and was not in a hurry. The world, he said, is full of free balance equipment, if only we are willing to notice it and to step carefully.

One bright Wednesday Mateo introduced Grace to his mother Rosa, a small, upright woman of seventy-eight who was moving through the slow, flowing postures of tai chi on the grass of Millfield Park. This gentle exercise, he explained, has good evidence behind it for reducing falls in older adults, and Rosa had been practising it for ten years. Rosa smiled, bowed slightly and invited Grace to come to her class on the following Wednesday, whether or not she had ever done anything of the kind.

Rosa's class met at ten on the grass beside the bandstand, and Grace joined a dozen others in a gentle circle, copying the teacher's slow movements as they shifted their weight and swept their arms through the air. She wobbled, laughed, lost her place and began again, and she noticed that by the end of the hour her mind was as quiet as her body was awake. Nobody minded the mistakes in the slightest, and when the class ended she walked home feeling lighter and smiling to herself.

After a month of daily practice, Grace stood on one leg in the middle of her lawn for a full twenty seconds without touching anything, her arms floating beside her like a pair of wings. Dorothy, standing at the fence with a cup of tea, timed her on a kitchen clock and gave a cheer. Nine of the ten moves had now been met, Mateo said, and only the last one was waiting.

Mateo gave her some sobering numbers, which he was careful to deliver gently: roughly one in three adults over sixty-five falls at least once a year, and the proportion rises in later decades. Most of these falls cause no serious harm, he said, but a minority lead to broken bones and a loss of confidence that can last far longer than the injury. That, he said, was exactly why prevention is worth every bit of the effort, and why they were sitting at the garden table that afternoon.

Falls, Mateo insisted, are not an unavoidable part of growing old, because most of them have causes that can be changed: weak muscles, poor balance, failing eyesight, certain medicines, and hazards in the home. Each one of these is something that a person can address, often quite cheaply, and each reduces the risk a little. A fall is rarely caused by one thing alone, he explained, which means that it can rarely be prevented by one thing alone either.

On Sunday afternoon Mateo and Grace made a slow tour of her house, looking at it as a tripping hazard rather than as a home. They found a loose rug in the hall, a cable trailing across the landing, a dim bulb at the top of the stairs and a slippery bathroom mat, and Grace felt embarrassed that she had never noticed them. Noticing, Mateo said kindly, is the whole point of the exercise, and nobody is born knowing how to do it.

Grace spent the following week putting things right: she took away the loose rug, clipped the cable along the skirting board, fitted brighter bulbs and plugged a little night light into the landing. In the bathroom she laid a non-slip mat, and Mateo helped her to fix a grab rail beside the bath. The house, she noticed, looked tidier, calmer and altogether more welcoming than it had before.

Mateo then turned his attention to footwear, and condemned Grace's flapping backless slippers as an invitation to disaster. Loose slippers and bare socks on a smooth floor are common causes of trips and slips, he said, and a close-fitting shoe or slipper with a firm sole and a good grip is far safer, both indoors and out. Grace found a new pair for twelve pounds, and she felt remarkably well-planted in them.

Vision, Mateo pointed out, plays a larger part in balance than most of us suppose, and changes in eyesight can raise the risk of a fall without our noticing. Grace booked an eye test, which she had been putting off for three years, and the optician reminded her that glasses with two strengths of lens can make the steps of a staircase look misleadingly close. She took a spare pair of single-vision glasses to wear for the stairs, which Mateo thought a very sensible idea indeed.

Mateo mentioned, with care, that some medicines can cause dizziness or drowsiness and so raise the chance of a fall, and that the effect can be stronger when several are taken together. Anyone with such a worry, he said, should talk to a pharmacist or a doctor, who can review the list, and nobody should ever stop a prescribed medicine on their own. Grace noted down two questions that she planned to ask at her next appointment, and she tucked the list into her handbag.

Occasionally, said Mateo, a person feels light-headed or sees stars on standing up too quickly, because blood pressure takes a moment to adjust. The sensible habit is to rise slowly, to pause for a breath with a hand on something sturdy and to move off only when the feeling has passed. Anyone who is often dizzy, or who ever faints, should see a doctor without delay, and Grace remembered her sit-to-stand and did it very slowly indeed.

The most reliable weapon of all, Mateo told her, is a programme that combines strength and balance exercises, and research has repeatedly shown that such programmes lower the risk of falls in older people, especially when they are kept up. Three sessions a week is a common aim, he said, but no figure should become a source of guilt. Grace looked at her list of ten moves and realised that she was already halfway through the best prescription there was.

Mateo drew a circle of arrows to explain the trap that catches so many people after a fright: fear of falling makes them move less, moving less makes them weaker, and weaker people fall more easily, which feeds the fear. The way to escape is not to stop being careful, he said, but to replace fear with strength and skill, bit by bit. Grace looked at the circle and saw, with some pride, that she had already stepped out of it.

One wet afternoon Mateo asked Grace a question that sounded quite innocent: when had she last sat on the floor? She laughed, then fell silent, and finally admitted that she could not remember a single occasion since the children were small. The tenth and last move, he said, was the one that most people forget they are losing, and it was the ability to get down to the floor and up again.

Getting down to the floor and up again, Mateo said, is a genuine skill that is lost without anyone noticing, since we spend so little time down there once we have grown up. It matters for play with children, for gardening and for ordinary tasks near the ground, and most of all because a person who knows how to get up is far less afraid of a fall. Skill, he said, is a quiet form of security, and it is one of the few that can be learned at any age.

They began by preparing the room as carefully as if for a small expedition: a thick exercise mat laid beside the sofa, which was too heavy to slide, a clear floor with no toys or rugs, and Mateo standing nearby. Grace should never practise this move, he said, when she was alone and unsure, until she had learned the pattern and her body had grown confident. Everyone needs a spotter at the beginning, he added, and there is no shame at all in asking someone to stay close.

The first stage of the descent, Mateo explained, was the half-kneel: place a hand on the seat of the sofa, step one foot back and lower the back knee gently to the mat while the front knee stays bent. Grace did it with her tongue between her teeth, and her heart beat rather fast. Seen from outside, said Mateo, it looked like a graceful, if slightly nervous, proposal of marriage.

From the half-kneel, said Mateo, she was to bring the second knee down beside the first, place both hands flat on the mat and lower her hip to one side until she was sitting. At each stage she was to pause, check that she was comfortable and breathe, since speed has no part in the move. The whole descent took Grace nearly a minute, and she enjoyed every second of it.

Once she was safely on the floor, Grace tried a few positions to see which felt best, with her legs stretched out, crossed or bent to one side, and Mateo told her that all were fine. The room looked quite different from down there, with the table legs towering overhead and a surprising quantity of dust under the sofa. She laughed aloud at the sight of it all, and Mateo, who was sitting cross-legged beside her by now, laughed along with her.

If her knees complained, Mateo said, she could slip a thick cushion beneath them, or rest her forearms on the sofa instead of putting her wrists on the floor, or choose a lower sofa to start from. Anyone with sore joints, a recent operation or any health problem, he added, should check first with a doctor or a physiotherapist before working on the floor. A good technique, he said, is simply one that works for the person doing it.

The following week, with Mateo standing beside the sofa and not touching her, Grace lowered herself to the mat unassisted, one careful stage after the next. When she finally sat down, flushed and delighted, Mateo gave a cheer that was heard two doors away, and Dorothy came to the window of number twelve to find out what was happening. It was only a woman sitting on a carpet, but it felt like an Olympic event.

On Saturday Anna brought Leo round, and the little boy marched into the living room clutching a box of wooden blocks, which he emptied across the carpet with a happy clatter. Grace felt a sudden longing to be down there among them, to build towers with him as she had once built them with his mother. She looked at Mateo's mat, took a deep breath and lowered herself carefully onto it.

For half an hour Grace and Leo built towers and bridges, knocked them down and rebuilt them, laughing as the wooden blocks tumbled across the carpet. Anna sat watching from the sofa with her coffee going cold, astonished to see her mother sitting comfortably on the floor, cross-legged and busy, as though it were the most natural thing in the world. Getting back up again, however, was a puzzle that Grace still had to solve.

When the tower had fallen for the last time, Grace looked up at the sofa, which suddenly seemed a long way off, and realised that she would have to get up. Mateo, who had been watching from the kitchen doorway with a smile, strolled over and said that there was nothing to fear, because the way back up was simply the way down in reverse. He promised to lead her through the movement in five calm steps, and to keep one hand near her at all times.

The first stage, said Mateo, was to roll onto her side and push herself up onto her hands and knees, in the position of a crawling baby. She was to stay there for a moment, breathing, and check that she felt well and that nothing hurt before she went any further. Grace crawled a little towards the sofa, and Leo crawled after her, roaring like a lion.

The second stage, Mateo said, was to crawl to something sturdy, such as a heavy sofa or a solid chair, and to place both hands flat on its seat. It had to be an object that would not tip or slide, and Grace tested the sofa with a firm push before she trusted it. Leo, who by now believed that this was a game invented entirely for his entertainment, tried to climb on her back.

The third stage was to bring the stronger leg forward and plant the foot flat on the floor, so that she knelt on one knee in front of the sofa with both hands still resting on the seat. It was the half-kneel again, only in reverse, and Grace found that her body remembered it perfectly. Mateo told her to take her time and to make sure that the front foot was well under the knee.

The fourth stage was the real effort: she pushed down through her hands and her front foot, let the thigh and buttock do the lifting, and rose steadily until she could turn and sit on the sofa. It felt like a very long rise, and her legs trembled, but she remembered the sit-to-stand, and the same muscles that had stood her up from the kitchen chair now did the work. She sat down at last with a great puff of breath, flushed and slightly damp with triumph, and Leo applauded.

Getting up from the floor, Grace discovered, is hard work for a beginner, and she sat on the sofa for a long minute, breathing slowly, while Leo built a tiny fort on her feet. Mateo told her that speed is quite unimportant and that the goal is a safe, controlled movement, not a race against the clock. She would be quicker in time, he said, but only if she did not try to be quick.

Over the next fortnight Grace practised the whole sequence of getting down and getting up three times each morning, with a cushion by the sofa and her mat on the carpet. Each repetition felt a little smoother than the last, and within a few days her legs had stopped trembling and her hands had stopped gripping the cushions so hard. She was learning the pattern, as Mateo had promised, and the pattern was learning her.

Mateo then taught her what to do after an unexpected fall, adding that this is general guidance and not a substitute for medical advice. She should stay calm, lie still for a moment and check carefully for pain before trying to move, and she should call for help at once if she thought that she was hurt. Never to hurry up in a panic, he stressed, was the first and most important rule.

If getting up proved impossible, Mateo said, the best course was to call out, use a phone or an alarm button to ask for help, and keep warm with a coat or a blanket while she waited. Lying on a cold floor for hours, he warned, is a danger in its own right, and this is why a phone should be kept in a pocket and not left on a side table. Grace slipped hers into her cardigan pocket at once, and she promised to keep it there from now on.

Mateo's final suggestion was to make a simple plan with the people close to her, so that if anything went wrong, somebody would know to look. Grace telephoned Anna that evening, told her about the exercises and agreed to ring every morning, and Dorothy at number twelve received a spare key to the house. The plan took half an hour to make and, said Mateo, was worth more than any amount of worry.

One bright morning Grace lowered herself to the living-room floor, rolled, crawled and rose again in one continuous and unhurried sequence, with nobody beside her but Leo, who was building a wall of blocks. The little boy clapped his hands and shouted that Granny had done it, and she realised that all ten moves now belonged to her. She sat on the sofa for a moment and let the thought sink in.

A few days later Mateo laid a blank calendar on the kitchen table and told Grace that the next task was to fit the ten moves into a real week, without turning her life into a second job. A plan, he said, is only useful if it is realistic, and a plan that is a little too easy is better than one that is a little too hard. He handed her a pencil and let her make the first choices herself, because a plan that belongs to you is a plan that you keep.

The shape of a good week, Mateo explained, was surprisingly simple: some walking on most days, strength exercises on two or three days, and a few minutes of balance practice daily, even if it was only the toothbrush trick. That combination, he said, matches the main advice in the official guidelines, and it can be rearranged to suit any life. Grace filled in the squares carefully and was surprised at how much space remained.

Every session, Mateo said, should begin with a warm-up of about five minutes, which prepares the body gradually for the work to come. Grace marched on the spot, swung her arms, rolled her shoulders and drew easy circles with her hips, until she felt warm and a little more alive. It was a short ritual, but it separated the business of exercise from the business of the rest of the day, and she grew fond of it.

At the end of each session Grace was to cool down, Mateo said, by walking slowly until her breathing and heartbeat returned to normal, then stretching the muscles she had used and drinking a glass of water. A cool-down is not a magic protection, he admitted, but it feels pleasant and gives the mind a clear signal that the work is done. Grace found that it was the part of the routine she looked forward to most.

By the end of the afternoon Grace had made her chart: walks on five days, strength sessions on Mondays and Thursdays, balance practice every day, the park hill on Saturdays and Sunday for rest. She stuck it on the fridge door beside the envelope with the original list of ten words. It looked almost professional, and for the first time in years she felt like a woman with a properly organised life.

Mateo defended the rest day against all attackers, because exercise, he said, is only the signal for the body to grow stronger, and the growing itself takes place afterwards, during rest. Grace should leave a free day between strength sessions, and she should treat a day of complete stillness as part of the programme and not as a failure. Rest, he said, is not the opposite of training but its other half, and the half that most keen beginners are inclined to skip.

Mateo drew a ladder of numbers from one to ten, where one was sitting in an armchair and ten was the hardest effort she could ever make. Moderate activity, he said, lay around five or six on that scale, with breathing deeper but speech still possible, while a hard effort was seven or eight. It was another way of using the talk test, and for many people it was easier to remember than a list of rules.

Grace took her notebook seriously now, and she added a gold star to the fridge chart for every day on which she moved, however little. Mateo approved, because a simple record gives a feeling of progress on days when the body feels no different and shows, over many weeks, the pattern of what really helps. Numbers are not the aim, he said, but they are an honest mirror, and they are a good deal kinder than memory.

Mateo was keen that Grace should not think of the ten moves as the whole of exercise, because swimming, cycling, dancing, bowls and gardening are all excellent and may suit some people better than others. The ten moves, he explained, are a base on which any other activity can stand, and the best activity of all is the one that a person looks forward to. Grace thought of the tea dance at the community hall and added it to the chart.

Winter arrived with dark mornings, frosted windows and a thin wind whistling down Linden Road, and for the first time in months Grace stood at the window with her walking shoes in her hand and no wish to go out. The cheerful certainty of the summer weeks had thinned, and the tick-boxes on the fridge chart seemed to be mocking her. It was, she decided, exactly the moment that Mateo had warned her about, and she knew that she would have to decide what to do.

Then Grace caught a heavy cold and spent a week in bed with tissues, hot lemon and a very bad temper. Mateo called round with soup and told her that rest is the right response to illness, that one lost week does not undo months of work, and that she should return gradually when she felt fully well. If she had a fever or chest symptoms, he added, she should wait until they were gone and ask a doctor if she was unsure.

When the cold had gone, Grace returned to her walking with a new humility, wearing a woolly hat and a thick scarf and keeping her route to half its former length. She built the time back up gradually over a fortnight, and she was relieved to find that her fitness had not entirely disappeared. The body, Mateo said, has a good memory for what it has learned, and it returns the favour of patience.

On icy mornings Grace took particular care, choosing shoes with a deep grip, shortening her steps, keeping to cleared paths and testing the surface before she trusted it with her whole weight. When the pavements were treacherous she did not go out at all, and she exercised indoors instead, which Mateo said was no surrender but good judgement. A fall on ice, he reminded her, would undo more than a week of walking could ever repay.

Mateo took the trouble to explain the difference between the sensations that accompany healthy exercise and those that are a warning of trouble. A dull ache in working muscles is normal and fades within a day or two, he said, whereas sharp pain, joint pain or pain that does not settle should make her stop and seek advice. The body's alarm signals, he added, are an excellent invention that should be heeded.

There were some signals, Mateo said gravely, that should never be ignored, and he listed them slowly so that she would remember: chest pain or pressure, severe breathlessness, fainting, or sudden weakness or numbness. Any of these meant stopping at once and getting urgent medical help, and he made certain that she knew the emergency number by heart. He hoped, he added, that she would never need it, and that the list was only a precaution.

In January Grace's right knee began to grumble, and Mateo adjusted her programme at once, lowering the height of her step-ups, shortening her walks and swapping the hill for a flat path. If the pain lasted more than a couple of weeks, or if the joint swelled or locked, he said, she should see her doctor or a physiotherapist and not simply wait. Fortunately for her, the knee settled within ten days, and the hill went back into the programme as soon as it was ready.

Mateo reminded her that sleep is the other half of training, since much of the body's repair work is done at night, and that a person short of sleep is more likely to feel low and skip her exercises. On some days an early night is a better investment than an extra hour of effort, he said, and nobody should feel guilty about choosing rest. Grace, for once, was entirely happy to take advice that sounded so pleasant, and she went to bed that night at nine.

Habits, said Mateo, are far easier to keep when they are attached to something that already happens each day, so Grace left her shoes beside the front door, walked after breakfast and balanced while the kettle boiled. Each of these small cues reminded her without any effort of will, and the chosen moment soon felt like part of the day. Motivation, he said, is overrated, and routine does most of the work for those of us who are not saints.

One morning in February the world woke up white, and Grace and Dorothy, wrapped in scarves and wearing their grippiest boots, walked very carefully round the park where the bare trees stood dusted with snow. The air was sharp and clean and almost entirely silent, and Grace realised with delight that winter had stopped being an enemy and become an adventure. Mateo, who had once called her consistent, was only half right, for by now she had also become delightfully stubborn.

In the spring Grace and Dorothy pinned a hand-written notice to the library board, inviting anyone who fancied an easy walk round Millfield Park to meet at the gates on Tuesday mornings at ten. Two people came to the first outing, Ken, a retired bus driver with a bad habit of telling jokes, and Priya, who lived at number five and had been hoping for someone to walk with. By the fourth week there were seven of them, and the Tuesday walkers had become something of a small local institution.

Mateo said that he was not at all surprised by the success of the club, since many studies suggest that people who exercise with others find it much easier to keep going. Friends offer encouragement, notice when you are missing and turn an effort into an outing, and the walk itself becomes a reason to see people as well as a means of keeping fit. Loneliness, he added, is a health risk of its own, and company is a kind of medicine.

When Anna came to stay for a long weekend she kept stopping in the middle of a sentence to stare, because her mother lifted a heavy flowerpot with a neat hinge and rose from the floor without using her hands. Anna had last seen her mother in the autumn, shaken and subdued, and the difference was so great that she hardly knew what to say. In the end she simply said, with tears in her eyes, that she was very proud of her mother, and Grace said that she was too.

On the bench in the evening Anna confessed that she had been frightened ever since the stumble, because she had thought of her grandmother and of all the things that can go wrong. Grace took her daughter's hand and explained, very gently, that falls can often be prevented and that she had never in her life felt so sure of her own legs. She did not promise that nothing could ever happen, only that she was doing everything she could.

One evening, when the others had gone home, Mateo told Grace why he had chosen his profession. As a boy of fourteen he had watched his grandfather lose his independence after a bad fall, and he had made up his mind that he would help other families to avoid the same loss. It was the kind of story that people tell only to their closest friends, and Grace listened to every word of it without once interrupting him.

At the end of the spring Rosa asked Grace to lead the warm-up at the tai chi class, and Grace, who had spent thirty-five years in front of a class, accepted with a laugh. She discovered that explaining each movement aloud made her understand it more fully, and that the new members, some of them nervous and some unsteady, looked at her with the same trust that her pupils once had. Teaching, she found with some amusement, is only learning with an audience, and she realised that she had missed having one.

Grace was invited to visit a class at the community hall where a group of people, some using walking frames and some in wheelchairs, were exercising from chairs with arm lifts, leg extensions and seated twists. It showed her that almost everyone can move in some way, and that a trained instructor or physiotherapist can adapt the exercises to a person's body, health and wishes. She came home determined to tell everyone she met, and to ask for advice before she suggested anything to anybody else.

In June, Dorothy stopped at the park fence and called out that she had found something. It was a poster for a five-kilometre community walk to be held in October, raising money to mend the old bandstand, and the Tuesday club voted at once, and almost without a joke from Ken, to enter as a team. Five kilometres was a good deal further than any of them had ever gone together, but nobody wanted to turn back.

All summer the Tuesday walkers lengthened their route by a few hundred metres at a time, moving from three kilometres to four and then, one glorious morning in September, to five, carrying water and resting on benches. Nobody was ever hurried along, and Mateo, who joined them when he could, said that this was the secret of success. A team, he said, goes at the pace of the people who need the most time, and nobody in it should ever feel like a burden.

On the night before the great walk, almost exactly a year after the stumble, Grace laid out her shoes, her yellow coat and her rucksack in the hall, as carefully as a soldier preparing for an inspection. In the kitchen she stopped in front of the fridge and looked at the envelope with its list of ten words, which had hung there since the Saturday that Mateo came to tea. She read it slowly, from walk to floor, and went to bed with a smile.

On the morning of the walk Millfield Park was a happy confusion of walkers in bright jackets, children with balloons, a brass band tuning up beside the bandstand and a table piled with paper numbers. Leo, who had turned five in the summer, wore a badge of his own and informed every stranger that his granny was going to walk the whole way. Grace pinned her number to her coat and found that her hands were quite steady.

At the sound of the whistle the Tuesday walkers moved off together, Ken telling a joke, Priya checking her watch, Dorothy in a new pair of walking shoes and Grace in her old yellow coat. They talked easily as they went, which Grace pointed out was the sign of a good brisk pace, and Dorothy said that she would have to find something to sing instead. Behind them the whole crowd streamed out of the park gates like a river.

The route led them down Linden Road, past the baker's with its warm smell of bread and the cherry tree at number eight, and as they approached the corner Grace realised where they were heading. Ahead of her, with the lamp post beside it, lay the very kerb on which she had caught her foot a year before. Her heart gave a small lurch, as it had done on that grey morning, though for a quite different reason.

Grace stepped down from the kerb, crossed the road and stepped up onto the opposite pavement in a single easy rhythm, her foot clearing the edge by a comfortable margin. Then she turned round, walked back and laid her hand for a moment on the cold iron of the lamp post that had once held her up. Dorothy, who knew the whole story and had heard it twice, said nothing at all but squeezed her arm very tightly and blew her nose.

The finish line was a banner stretched between two trees at the edge of the park, and Grace walked under it to a ripple of cheering, with Leo running beside her, his badge flapping on his chest. Anna, who had been waiting there since the first walkers set off, threw her arms round them both and cried a little into her mother's shoulder. Five kilometres had taken them just under an hour, and she would not have swapped a single minute of it for anything.

Afterwards the club sat in a row on the grass beside the bandstand with tea in paper cups and slices of lemon cake, comparing blisters and boasting shamelessly. The organiser announced through a megaphone that the day's walkers had raised enough to start the first repairs, and the brass band played a tune that Rosa swore she had danced to in 1962. Grace had never in her life felt so pleasantly tired, or so thoroughly and completely happy, and she said so to nobody in particular.

Sitting on the grass with his empty cup, Mateo counted the ten moves on his fingers, from the walk to the floor, and reminded Grace how far she had come since the day she grabbed the lamp post. She was not an athlete, he said with a smile, and she had never needed to be, because she was something far more useful: a woman who was strong, steady and unafraid. Grace looked down at her hands, which had pulled and pushed and carried so much that year, and she knew that every word was true.

That evening Grace sat on the living-room floor with Leo curled in her lap, reading him a story about a bear who could not sleep, and when the last page was turned she rose in a single smooth movement. Anna, who was watching from the sofa, was quite certain that she had seen a small miracle, although to Grace it was now just the ordinary business of a day. That, she thought, was exactly what the ten moves were meant to achieve: to make the extraordinary things ordinary again.

Priya's older sister, who had watched the finish from the edge of the crowd, asked Grace quietly how she had done it, and Grace took the old envelope with its list of ten words from her bag. She said that she had been given the list a year ago by a good friend, and that the only advice she could add was to start smaller than you think you should and to be patient with yourself. Then she asked the woman to pass the list on when she had finished with it.

Walk, stand, bend, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and rise from the floor: these ten moves are the ordinary movements of a lifetime, and a little practice each day helps to keep them yours. Start gently, listen to your body and be patient, because strength and balance can improve at any age.
